issues.title: Empirically justify TL loop timeout defaults from real latency data instead of picking round numbers
issues.description:
Question: 

Context: 

Findings:

comments.content:
RESEARCH SPEC — follow exactly. Context: linked to #916 (exposing the 5 TL-loop timeout constants as config). While writing #916, the operator noted the current default values (10s transport, 30s ledger active-tail, 5s dispatch, 300s controller stall, 30s idle) were never actually justified by anything — round numbers picked without evidence. This issue is about producing that evidence and a stated methodology. It is explicitly NOT about changing any default itself — see DONE CRITERIA.

## GOAL
For each of the five constants #916 makes configurable, determine what real-world duration distribution it is actually bounding, gather a genuine sample of that distribution, and derive a candidate default from a percentile + margin rather than intuition. Record the methodology and result per-constant as a decision comment on this issue. Changing any actual default in code is an explicit separate follow-up (a human reviews the evidence and decides; this issue produces the evidence, not the code change).

## THE FIVE CONSTANTS AND WHAT EACH ONE ACTUALLY BOUNDS
1. `tl_transport_timeout_seconds` (default 10.0, transport.py) — the UDS RPC round-trip from the Python controller to the local `exomonad serve` process for one `/agents/tl/root/tools/call` request. This is a network-adjacent (local socket) call, not raw compute — its tail is set by how slow the *slowest* effect handler behind any single tool call can be (e.g. `poll_workers`'s per-agent `chainlink issue show` subprocess fan-out, or a `git`/`gh` call inside `spawn_leaf`/`merge_pr`), not by socket latency itself.
2. `tl_active_tail_timeout_seconds` (default 30.0, events/queue.py) — the max gap `LedgerQueue` tolerates between successive reads reaching a new segment tail before it decides the tailer has stalled. Bounds local filesystem read/poll cadence, not network.
3. `tl_dispatch_timeout_seconds` (default 5.0, driver.py) — per tl_loop/CLAUDE.md § "Durable child-dispatch protocol," bounds *only the transport operation* of a spawn request (i.e., overlaps conceptually with #1 but is checked at a different call site — confirm during investigation whether it's actually redundant with #1 or measures something distinct, e.g. a different code path/timeout wrapper).
4. `tl_controller_stall_timeout_seconds` (default 300.0, driver.py) — NOT the same kind of thing as 1-3. This bounds how long the controller waits with no progress before emitting a `wave.stalled` observation (heartbeat.py:173-189) — it's a "how patient should we be waiting on a human/agent" tolerance, not a machine-speed-scaled operation latency. Flag explicitly in your findings whether this constant even belongs in a latency-percentile methodology at all, or whether it's a policy choice orthogonal to machine speed.
5. `tl_idle_timeout_seconds` (default 30.0, __main__.py/driver.py) — controls polling/wait cadence in the idle loop; clarify exactly what operation's absence-of-progress it's measuring during investigation (read the call sites, don't assume from the name).

## ANTI-PATTERNS (DO NOT)
- DO NOT change any default value as part of this issue. This issue's output is a decision record (data + methodology + a recommended number per constant with reasoning), not a code diff. A default change is a separate, explicitly human-approved follow-up issue that cites this one's findings.
- DO NOT invent a synthetic/simulated load test as the *only* evidence source. Prefer real historical data from actual runs (see DATA SOURCES) — synthetic benchmarks may not reflect what a real slow machine (like the one that motivated #916) actually experiences (real chainlink DB size, real git history size, real disk contention from other processes).
- DO NOT treat all five constants with one uniform methodology. #1-3 are latency-bound (percentile-of-observed-duration is the right frame); #4 is a patience/policy choice; #5 needs its exact semantics confirmed before deciding which frame applies. Say explicitly which frame you used for each.
- DO NOT require live Tempo/Grafana to be running as a hard prerequisite — this project's `controller-output.log` files already contain enough timestamped INFO-level request/response pairs (see DATA SOURCES) to do meaningful percentile analysis offline, right now, without deploying anything. Use Tempo/OTel as the *better* source when available, log-mining as the always-available fallback.
- DO NOT pick a margin policy (e.g. "2x p99") without stating it explicitly and explaining why. An unstated margin is exactly the kind of undocumented heuristic this project's CLAUDE.md rules out ("Always prefer failure to an undocumented heuristic or fallback").

## DATA SOURCES (in order of preference)
1. **OTel/Tempo, if running.** `rust/exomonad-core/src/effects/mod.rs:158` already has `#[instrument(skip_all, fields(effect_type = %effect_type, ..., agent_name = %ctx.agent_name))]` on the generic effect-dispatch path — every effect call already produces a span with duration, tagged by `effect_type`. Per CLAUDE.md § Tempo Observability, query with:
       curl -s 'http://localhost:3200/api/search?q=%7B+span.effect_type+%3D+%22poll_workers%22+%7D&limit=200&spss=200'
   Extract span durations per `effect_type` (esp. `poll_workers`, `spawn_leaf`, `merge_pr`) to characterize constants #1 and #3's real distribution. This does NOT cover #2 (`tl_active_tail_timeout_seconds`) — that's a pure-Python local file-read cadence with no Rust span; see source 2.
2. **`controller-output.log` timestamp mining (always available, zero new instrumentation).** Every `.exo/tl-loop/<run_id>/controller-output.log` (this repo's own historical runs, and — with the operator's permission, since it's a separate project's data — the accumulated beast-workspace history we already inspected this session) has INFO lines like:
       2026-08-19 22:54:03,337 INFO [TL loop transport] request method=POST path=/agents/tl/root/tools/call ...
       2026-08-19 22:54:03,412 INFO [TL loop transport] response method=POST path=/agents/tl/root/tools/call status=200 size=...
   Pairing consecutive request/response lines by timestamp gives real UDS RPC durations (constant #1) directly, across every historical run already on disk, with no new code. `"waiting observation"` log lines' inter-arrival gaps approximate the idle/heartbeat cadence (constant #5). Write a small offline script (Python stdlib only, matching tl_loop's own dependency discipline) that globs `.exo/tl-loop/*/controller-output.log*`, parses these pairs, and reports percentiles — this script is a reusable artifact of this issue, not throwaway.
3. **New lightweight instrumentation, only where 1+2 don't cover the constant.** Constant #2 (`tl_active_tail_timeout_seconds`) has no existing timing signal anywhere (`LedgerQueue`'s tail-read loop doesn't log its own cadence). If historical data can't answer it, add a single DEBUG-level log line recording gap duration on each tail read in `tl_loop/events/queue.py`, run a representative session to collect samples, then remove or downgrade the added logging noise once the constant is set (or keep it at DEBUG permanently if it's cheap and useful — your call, but state the decision).

## STEPS
1. For each constant, confirm its exact call site and what operation it wraps (read the code, don't trust this spec's summary blindly — especially for #3 vs #1 overlap, and #5's precise semantics).
2. Gather real duration samples via the data sources above, preferring #1/#2 over #3.
3. Compute p50/p95/p99 (or best available given sample size — note sample size and its limitations explicitly if small).
4. State a margin policy per constant (can differ per constant if justified) and derive a candidate default.
5. Record all of this — methodology, raw percentile numbers, sample size/source, margin policy, and the resulting candidate default — as a `--kind decision` comment on this issue, one per constant or one consolidated comment covering all five.
6. Do not touch any source file's actual default value.
7. If any constant's investigation concludes "not enough real data exists yet to justify a number better than the current one," say so explicitly rather than forcing a number — that is a valid, honest outcome for that constant.

## READ FIRST
- #916 (the config-exposure issue this is linked to — read its full spec, especially the per-constant table)
- tl_loop/client/transport.py, tl_loop/events/queue.py, tl_loop/loop/driver.py:470-509, tl_loop/loop/heartbeat.py:90-209 (exact semantics of each constant)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/effects/mod.rs:150-170 (the existing `#[instrument]` span this issue's Tempo-based analysis would query)
- CLAUDE.md § Tempo Observability (TraceQL query syntax, ports, docker compose)
- Any `.exo/tl-loop/*/controller-output.log*` files already on disk in this repo's own dev history, if any exist, as a first real (if small) sample before asking the operator for access to other projects' logs

## VERIFY
- The offline log-mining script (if written) runs cleanly against at least one real `controller-output.log` and produces a percentile table.
- Every one of the five constants has either a stated candidate default + evidence, or an explicit "insufficient data" conclusion — no constant left unaddressed.
- No source file outside this issue's own reusable analysis script (if any) is modified.

## DONE CRITERIA
- A decision record exists on this issue covering all five constants: methodology used, data source, sample size, computed percentiles (where applicable), margin policy, and candidate default (or explicit "insufficient evidence").
- The reusable log-mining script (if produced) is placed somewhere sensible (e.g. `scripts/` or `tl_loop/tools/`) and documented, not left as a one-off.
- No default values changed in this issue — that is explicitly a follow-up issue citing these findings, filed only after a human reviews them.

issues.title: Expose TL loop timeouts (transport, ledger tail, dispatch, stall, idle) as config so slower machines can raise them
issues.description:
Goal: 

Acceptance criteria:
-

comments.content:
WORKER SPEC — follow exactly. Context: confirmed by the operator that real transport timeouts occurred on a slower machine (not reproduced on this one, which is faster). `origin/snapshot/a01e72d3` ("feat: configure TL transport timeout") is a real one-off fix for exactly one of these constants, made while debugging on that machine — use it as a reference/scaffold for the pattern, but do NOT cherry-pick it wholesale (see ANTI-PATTERNS).

## GOAL
Every hardcoded TL-loop timeout/interval constant that scales with machine speed (disk I/O, subprocess spawn cost, socket round-trip) should be operator-configurable via `.exo/config.toml`, following the exact plumbing pattern `a01e72d3` already proved out for one field: Rust `Config`/`RawConfig` field (validated `> 0`, local > global > default resolution) → threaded into the generated TL-window command as a CLI flag in `rust/exomonad/src/init.rs` → `argparse` flag in `tl_loop/__main__.py` → into the relevant Python constructor. Defaults must NOT change — this machine's defaults are fine; the point is giving a slower machine a lever, not changing anyone's out-of-the-box behavior.

## SURVEYED CANDIDATES (confirmed by grep, not exhaustive — verify no others exist during READ FIRST)
1. `tl_loop/client/transport.py:14` `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 10.0` — UDS RPC call timeout to the local exomonad server. This is what `a01e72d3` addressed. Reuse its Rust/CLI/argparse plumbing pattern exactly, but do NOT carry over its change to the Python default (it bumped `DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` from 10.0 to 120.0 — revert that hunk; the constant stays 10.0, only becomes overridable).
2. `tl_loop/events/queue.py:23` `DEFAULT_ACTIVE_TAIL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 30.0` — the ledger tailer's active-tail timeout, threaded into `LedgerQueue` but never passed a non-default value from `tl_loop/__main__.py:187` (`LedgerQueue(reader, poll_interval=args.poll_interval)` — no `active_tail_timeout` kwarg at all today). NOT exposed at any layer currently. Directly relevant: an earlier crash in this operator's own beast-workspace history (`.exo/tl-loop/root.invalid-1786975775254/controller-exit.json`) recorded `"reason": "ledger tailer stopped"` — a plausible symptom of this exact timeout being too tight on a slow machine. Highest-value addition in this issue.
3. `tl_loop/loop/driver.py:482` `dispatch_timeout: float = 5.0` on `TLLoopConfig` — "bounds only the transport operation" per tl_loop/CLAUDE.md § Durable child-dispatch protocol (does not itself fail the slice, but a too-tight value produces spurious `dispatch_unconfirmed` states and reconciliation churn on a slow machine). No CLI flag, no config.toml path — only reachable by constructing `TLLoopConfig` directly (tests only).
4. `tl_loop/loop/driver.py:483` `controller_stall_timeout: float = 300.0` — same story, no CLI/config path today.
5. `tl_loop/__main__.py:38` `DEFAULT_IDLE_TIMEOUT = 30.0` / `driver.py:480` `idle_timeout: float = 30.0` — DOES have a CLI flag already (`--idle-timeout`, `_run()` threads `args.idle_timeout` into `TLLoopConfig`), but `rust/exomonad/src/init.rs`'s `tl_loop_command()` never passes `--idle-timeout` when building the TL window's launch command, and there is no `.exo/config.toml` field for it — so today an operator cannot actually set it through the supported `exomonad init` path at all, only by hand-editing the generated tmux command. This one needs only the Rust-side half of the plumbing (config field + CLI-flag threading in init.rs); the Python CLI flag and TLLoopConfig wiring already exist.

## ANTI-PATTERNS (DO NOT)
- DO NOT change any existing default value. Every constant listed above keeps its current number; only the ability to override it via `.exo/config.toml` is new. Verify this explicitly with a test that asserts unset-config behavior is byte-identical to current behavior for every field.
- DO NOT cherry-pick `a01e72d3` as a merge/cherry-pick commit. Use it as a read-only reference for the pattern (Rust field shape, validation, test style) and reimplement cleanly across all five fields with consistent naming, since the original commit only covers #1 and changes its default (see #1 above).
- DO NOT collapse all five into a single "global timeout multiplier" or one shared knob — they bound different operations with different legitimate scales (a 10s RPC timeout and a 300s controller stall timeout are not the same axis), and a single knob would force one machine-speed correction to apply unevenly across unrelated operations. Keep them as five independent, separately named fields.
- DO NOT invent a sixth "auto-detect machine speed" heuristic. This is operator-set configuration, not an adaptive system — consistent with this project's "always prefer failure to an undocumented heuristic" rule.
- DO NOT widen validation beyond `> 0` (matches `a01e72d3`'s existing `tl_transport_timeout_seconds <= 0.0` bail check) — no upper bound, no unit conversion magic.

## READ FIRST
- `git show a01e72d3` (or `git show origin/snapshot/a01e72d3`) for the full reference pattern — Rust `RawConfig`/`Config` field addition, `DEFAULT_TL_TRANSPORT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS` const, validation, `tl_loop_command()` threading in `rust/exomonad/src/init.rs`, `tl_loop/__main__.py` argparse flag, `TransportClient` constructor threading, and its Rust + Python tests (`rust/exomonad/src/config.rs::test_raw_config_parse_tl_transport_timeout`, `tl_loop/tests/test_main.py::test_run_passes_transport_timeout_to_client`) — use these as the literal template for the other four fields.
- `rust/exomonad/src/config.rs` (RawConfig/Config struct, resolution order, Default impl, existing tests)
- `rust/exomonad/src/init.rs` (`tl_loop_command`, its call site in `run()`, its existing test `tl_loop_command_uses_programmatic_controller`)
- `rust/exomonad/src/revert.rs` (test fixture `Config` literal that must stay exhaustive — `a01e72d3` had to update this too when it added a field)
- `tl_loop/__main__.py` (`_parser()`, `_run()`, `DEFAULT_IDLE_TIMEOUT`)
- `tl_loop/client/transport.py` (`DEFAULT_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, `TransportClient.__init__`)
- `tl_loop/events/queue.py` (`DEFAULT_ACTIVE_TAIL_TIMEOUT_SECONDS`, `LedgerQueue.__init__`)
- `tl_loop/loop/driver.py:470-509` (`TLLoopConfig` dataclass — `dispatch_timeout`, `controller_stall_timeout`, `idle_timeout` fields)
- `tl_loop/CLAUDE.md` § "Durable child-dispatch protocol" (dispatch_timeout's documented semantics — must not change)
- `CLAUDE.md` § Configuration table (where to document the five new fields, matching existing field doc style)

## STEPS
1. Rust: add five `Option<f64>` (or `Option<u64>` where the field is naturally an integer count — check each Python default's type) fields to `RawConfig`, five resolved fields to `Config`, five `DEFAULT_TL_*_SECONDS` constants, local>global>default resolution, and `> 0` validation for each — mirroring exactly what `a01e72d3` did for `tl_transport_timeout_seconds`. Field names: `tl_transport_timeout_seconds` (keep, default 10.0, drop the 120.0 change), `tl_active_tail_timeout_seconds` (default 30.0), `tl_dispatch_timeout_seconds` (default 5.0), `tl_controller_stall_timeout_seconds` (default 300.0), `tl_idle_timeout_seconds` (default 30.0).
2. Rust: extend `tl_loop_command()` in `init.rs` to accept and pass all five as CLI flags (`--transport-timeout`, `--active-tail-timeout`, `--dispatch-timeout`, `--controller-stall-timeout`, `--idle-timeout`), update its call site and its existing test.
3. Rust: update `revert.rs`'s test `Config` literal (and any other exhaustive `Config { .. }` literal — grep for `orphan_reconciler_interval_secs:` as a marker, since that's the field immediately preceding `a01e72d3`'s addition point, to find every struct literal that needs the new fields).
4. Python: add the four missing `argparse` flags to `tl_loop/__main__.py`'s `run` subcommand (`--active-tail-timeout`, `--dispatch-timeout`, `--controller-stall-timeout`; `--idle-timeout` already exists), thread `args.active_tail_timeout` into the `LedgerQueue(...)` call (currently missing the kwarg entirely), and `args.dispatch_timeout`/`args.controller_stall_timeout` into the `TLLoopConfig(...)` construction alongside the existing `idle_timeout=args.idle_timeout`.
5. Update `CLAUDE.md`'s Configuration table with all five fields, following the existing doc-comment style (see `tl_transport_timeout_seconds`'s entry from `a01e72d3` as the template) and this project's rule to always update CLAUDE.md alongside behavior changes.

## TESTS TO ADD (CI-covered — required, not optional)
- Rust: one `test_raw_config_parse_tl_*_timeout` per new field (parse from TOML), one assertion per field in the "defaults" test that its resolved value equals the existing hardcoded default when unset (mirrors `test_raw_config_parse_model_field`-style tests already in `config.rs`).
- Rust: extend `tl_loop_command_uses_programmatic_controller` (or add a sibling test) asserting all five `--*-timeout` flags appear in the generated command with their passed values.
- Python: extend `tl_loop/tests/test_main.py::test_run_passes_transport_timeout_to_client` (or add three siblings) proving `--active-tail-timeout`, `--dispatch-timeout`, `--controller-stall-timeout` each reach their respective constructor (`LedgerQueue`, `TLLoopConfig`) — same `monkeypatch`-and-capture pattern already used for `transport_timeout`.
- Python: one regression test in `tl_loop/tests/` asserting that omitting every new CLI flag reproduces today's exact defaults end to end (10.0 / 30.0 / 5.0 / 300.0 / 30.0) — the "no default changed" guarantee from ANTI-PATTERNS, made explicit and CI-enforced rather than just eyeballed in review.
- Ensure all of the above run under the project's standard CI gate (`just test` / `just pre-commit` per this repo's CI workflow) — do not add a new ad hoc test entrypoint.

## VERIFY
- cargo test -p exomonad config:: init::   (or `just rust-test` scoped)
- tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tl_loop/tests
- tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m ruff check tl_loop
- just pre-commit
- Manually generate a `.exo/config.toml` setting all five fields to non-default values, run `exomonad init` (in a scratch project), and confirm the TL window's actual launched command line (via `tmux list-panes` / the recorded command) carries every flag with the configured value.

## DONE CRITERIA
- All five constants are configurable via `.exo/config.toml`, following one consistent naming/plumbing pattern.
- Every default is unchanged from today (10.0 / 30.0 / 5.0 / 300.0 / 30.0) when unset — CI-proven, not just asserted in the PR description.
- `origin/snapshot/a01e72d3` is not merged as-is; its useful pattern is reflected in the new code, its default-bump is not.
- CLAUDE.md documents all five fields.
- Full test suite (`just pre-commit`) green.

INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION (2026-08-20): ea10a030 correctly rejects NaN in Rust and Python while preserving the issue's literal >0 policy; the exact Rust regression passes, the full Python suite passes 450 tests, and Ruff is clean. 72e7606a correctly narrows the timeout capture fixture. #916 remains complete.

issues.title: TL controller heartbeat crashes on 'poll_workers result has no workers array' racing a leaf's own exit
issues.description:
Steps to reproduce:
1. 

Expected: 
Actual:

comments.content:
WORKER SPEC — follow exactly. Prior context: discovered live in beast-workspace/workspace tonight, ~15 min after `exomonad init --recreate` (fresh binary/WASM/tl_loop.pyz install, ruled out as stale — see CONFIRMED below).

## SYMPTOM
The TL controller (run_id=root) died with:
    HeartbeatError: poll_workers result has no workers array
`controller-exit.json` recorded_at=1787198103.666898 (2026-08-19 22:55:03 local). tmux window for the controller is gone; only Server and Watcher panes remain in the session.

## CONFIRMED
- Everything was freshly rebuilt/reinstalled minutes before the crash: `~/.cargo/bin/exomonad`, `~/.exo/wasm/wasm-guest-devswarm.wasm`, and the project-local copy in beast-workspace/.exo/wasm/, and `~/.exo/tl_loop.pyz` all share mtimes in the 22:41:10-22:43:19 window, all after `git log -1` on this repo (50d916ae). Not a stale-install skew.
- `PollWorkers.hs` (haskell/wasm-guest/src/ExoMonad/Guest/Tools/PollWorkers.hs:76-85), on the success path (`pollWorkersCore` returning `Right`), unconditionally includes `"workers" .= rows` in the returned object — `rows` is `[Value]` from `forM agents (agentPollRow ...)` and serializes as a JSON array even when `agents` is empty (`[]`, not absent). So per current source, a genuine `Right` return from `pollWorkersCore` cannot produce a payload lacking a `workers` array.
- `tl_loop/loop/heartbeat.py:265-269` (`_result_object`) checks `result.success is False` FIRST and raises a *different* message ("poll_workers returned failure") in that case. The crash message we got ("... has no workers array", heartbeat.py:234) is only reachable when `result.success` was True AND `result.result` was a Mapping AND that mapping's `"workers"` key was missing or non-list. That combination is inconsistent with the Haskell success path described above.
- Exact-second correlation: the dev-leaf's own invocation record (`.exo/agents/tunable-operator-body-opencode/invocation.json`, generation 5) shows `"ended_at": 1787198103, "status": "exited", "exit_code": 0` — a clean, expected one-shot exit (per this project's documented one-shot coding-invocation model) — at the SAME epoch second the controller's heartbeat crashed (recorded_at 1787198103.666898, ~0.67s later). The controller's own log shows this was the first `poll_workers`-shaped call of that heartbeat tick (a single request/response pair, size=1750, vs. two request/response pairs of sizes 289+510 on the two preceding successful ticks).

## LEADING HYPOTHESIS (not yet proven — needs reproduction)
A race between a leaf's normal exit (which tears down its tmux window, per `.exo/agents/{name}/routing.json`'s `window_id`) and a concurrent `poll_workers` heartbeat call that is, at that same instant, resolving that same agent's window/pane liveness. Something in that path — most likely the Rust `session.list_agents` handler (rust/exomonad-core/src/handlers/session.rs:225, `list_agents`) or its liveness resolution (`resolve_agent_liveness`, referenced from `services/continuation/composer.rs` and elsewhere) — either (a) throws/returns an error for the just-closed window that isn't correctly propagated as `success: false` through the REST→Python `ToolResult` boundary (making Python see a "successful" but malformed/incomplete payload), or (b) races a WASM-level uncaught exception in `pollWorkersCore`'s `agentPollRow`/`chainlinkIssueShowCore` calls that bypasses the `Left`/`Right` modeling entirely and falls through to some generic non-tool-shaped error envelope Rust returns for an unhandled WASM failure.

This is a real, by-design-reproducible failure mode, not a one-off: leaves exiting mid-heartbeat is normal and frequent (one-shot invocations exit as soon as they publish a PR), and every such exit races against whatever heartbeat interval is configured. A controller that can be killed by its own routine liveness poll racing a leaf's normal, successful exit is a severe availability bug — it doesn't require anything to actually go wrong with the leaf's work.

## ANTI-PATTERNS (DO NOT)
- DO NOT patch this by making `_poll_workers` in heartbeat.py swallow a missing `workers` key and treat it as an empty list — that would silently hide a real transport/effect-boundary bug and could mask agents going permanently unpolled.
- DO NOT add a retry-and-ignore around the `poll_workers` call without first identifying which side (Rust session.rs, WASM PollWorkers.hs, or the REST/JSON envelope translation) actually produced the malformed payload — retrying blind risks reproducing #911's pattern (symptom patched without root cause identified).
- DO NOT assume this is the same bug as #911 (that one was a schema/state-writer ordering bug, fully unrelated code path) — verify independently.

## READ FIRST
- tl_loop/loop/heartbeat.py:90-269 (full heartbeat cycle, `_poll_workers`, `_result_object`)
- haskell/wasm-guest/src/ExoMonad/Guest/Tools/PollWorkers.hs (full file — especially `pollWorkersCore`, `agentPollRow`, `toolHandlerEff`)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/handlers/session.rs:225-onward (`list_agents`)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/handlers/agent.rs — `resolve_agent_liveness` and how a window that has just closed is classified (dead vs error)
- rust/exomonad-core/CLAUDE.md § "Agent Resume and Liveness Contract" (routing.json retention semantics, exited_at/invocation.json as retirement markers) — the liveness check may be reading routing state for a window mid-teardown in a way that wasn't anticipated by that contract
- tl_loop/client/effects.py (`poll_workers` method, ~line 278) and whatever REST/JSON-RPC translation sits between it and the Haskell tool response — confirm the shape Python actually receives vs what Haskell sends, to rule out an envelope-unwrapping bug vs a genuine Rust/Haskell-side failure

## STEPS
1. Reproduce deterministically: spawn a leaf, let it reach its normal one-shot exit, and trigger (or wait for) a heartbeat's `poll_workers` call to land within the same ~1s window as the exit. A tight test harness can force this by calling the `poll_workers` MCP tool directly (bypassing the heartbeat scheduler) immediately after killing/closing a spawned agent's tmux window, to isolate whether the bug is in the Rust/Haskell tool response itself (reproducible without the Python heartbeat loop at all) or only manifests through the heartbeat's specific call pattern.
2. Once reproduced at the tool-call level, add logging/tracing (per this project's CLAUDE.md § Logging — log request/response at the effect boundary) to capture the raw REST response body for a `poll_workers` call made during this exact race window, and compare it against a normal successful response to find exactly which field or top-level shape differs.
3. Trace whether the fault is: (a) an uncaught exception inside WASM (would show as a host-level panic/error log distinct from `errorResult`), (b) a Rust handler returning a `success: false` envelope that Python's transport layer is misreading as success, or (c) a genuine race in `resolve_agent_liveness`/window-liveness reads that returns a differently-shaped (not error, just malformed) response for a window mid-close.
4. Fix at the identified layer. If the root cause is "querying a window that's mid-teardown produces inconsistent state," the fix likely belongs in the Rust liveness resolution (treat a window-not-found-during-teardown as a normal dead/retired state, not an error) — but confirm before assuming.
5. Add a regression test that reproduces the race deterministically (spawn + immediately close/kill window + poll_workers call) rather than relying on timing.

## VERIFY
- The new regression test fails against pre-fix code and passes after the fix.
- just rust-test and the WASM guest test suite stay green.
- tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tl_loop/tests -k heartbeat stays green.
- Manually confirm in beast-workspace (or an equivalent fixture) that a controller survives a heartbeat tick landing within the same second as a leaf's normal exit, across several repeated runs (race conditions need more than one clean pass to trust).

## DONE CRITERIA
- Root cause identified and documented (which layer, which exact code path) — not just patched around.
- Regression test proves the race no longer crashes the controller.
- A leaf's normal, successful one-shot exit can never kill the TL controller via a concurrent poll_workers heartbeat.
- Full test suite green.

ROOT CAUSE IDENTIFIED + FIX — different from the leading liveness-race hypothesis.

## Root cause (layer + exact code path)

The malformed payload was NOT a WASM exception, NOT a Rust success:false misread, and NOT a liveness-race in resolve_agent_liveness. It is the unread-mail piggyback at the REST envelope boundary:

- rust/exomonad/src/serve.rs `call_tool` ran `append_unread_mail_block(&mut output, ...)` on EVERY successful tool call when the caller had unread inbox mail.
- `append_unread_mail_block` replaces `output.result` with `{"content": [...], "isError": false}` whenever the result isn't already MCP-content-shaped (serve.rs:1154-1158).
- The programmatic TL controller (`tl_loop/client/transport.py` -> `ToolResult.from_raw`) consumes the RAW `{success, result, error}` envelope and reads `result["workers"]` directly. When a leaf exited and its `notify_parent` landed unread mail in the controller inbox, the next heartbeat's `poll_workers` succeeded (`success: true`), then got its structured result clobbered to `{content, isError}`, so `payload.get("workers")` was None -> 'poll_workers result has no workers array'.

This explains the exact-second correlation: leaf one-shot exit -> notify_parent -> unread mail in controller inbox -> next poll_workers tick hits the piggyback. The liveness query itself was fine.

## Fix

Gate the mail piggyback behind an explicit `x-exomonad-mail-piggyback` request header that only the mcp-stdio binary sends (rust/exomonad/src/uds_client.rs). Raw REST callers (tl_loop) now receive the unmodified structured result. mcp-stdio (Claude Code agents) keeps the mail piggyback.

- control.rs: new `MAIL_PIGGYBACK_HEADER` constant
- uds_client.rs: ServerClient::call_tool/raw_post sends the header
- serve.rs: extracted `maybe_append_unread_mail` that no-ops without the header

## Regression test

serve.rs `mail_piggyback_requires_mcp_stdio_header`: proves a raw caller (no header) keeps the `workers` key intact while an mcp-stdio caller (with header) still gets unread mail appended. cargo test -p exomonad green (102), heartbeat pytest green (5).

REOPENED + strengthened the regression test. Extracted finalize_tool_response() (the exact {success, result, error} envelope the controller parses) out of call_tool, and the new test poll_workers_result_survives_unread_mail_for_raw_controller now drives a poll_workers-shaped result through that envelope with a real in-memory InboxStore seeded by a simulated leaf notify_parent, asserting the raw (header-less) controller keeps the 'workers' key intact while the mcp-stdio (header) caller still gets the mail block. Verified cargo test -p exomonad (102) and clippy clean.

issues.title: Wire a difficulty/attempt-aware model catalog into select_model() and TL dispatch

comments.content:
DESIGN + IMPLEMENTATION SPEC. Context: subissue of #912 (see parent for full diagnosis). Sequence after #913 lands (that fix is what makes any model this issue computes actually reach the spawned agent) — this issue's Python-side work can be developed in parallel, but is not observably correct until #913 merges.

## PROBLEM
`tl_loop/select/model.py::select_model(harness, catalog, requested_model, ...)` only resolves an already-known model *reference string* against a `ModelCatalog` (exact → alias → dated → provider_default → fallback-to-first). Nothing in the codebase computes that `requested_model` string from a slice's difficulty or attempt history, and `TLLoopConfig.catalog` is never populated outside tests, so the function never runs in production (driver.py:3918 gates the call on `config.catalog is not None`, which is always false live). Meanwhile `tl_loop/select/agent_type.py::select_harness` already computes exactly the signal this needs — `classify_task()` → `Difficulty`, plus `slice.attempts`/`slice.verdict` — but only spends it on harness escalation (agent_type.py:167-198), never on model tier.

## ANTI-PATTERNS (DO NOT)
- DO NOT invent a new difficulty classifier — reuse `classify_task()` (tl_loop/select/classify.py) and its `Classification.difficulty`/`matched_rule_name`; it is already deterministic and explainable, which this project requires (see classify.py module docstring).
- DO NOT let this widen `.exo/harness_policy.toml`'s allowlist or any budget ceiling — model tier selection must stay inside the same human-authored allow/cost_rank/token_budget boundary the harness selector already respects (see harness_policy.toml comments and CLAUDE.md § "Structured plans and bounded judgment": "The selector applies .exo/harness_policy.toml and capability ratings without widening an allowlist or ceiling").
- DO NOT hardcode a difficulty→model_id table with vendor-specific model names inside tl_loop/select — that duplicates the model catalog's job. The mapping should be difficulty→abstract tier (e.g. cheap/standard/strong) resolved against whatever catalog is actually loaded, the same way `select_model`'s existing alias/dated/provider_default rungs are catalog-driven rather than hardcoded.
- DO NOT change `#913`'s fix or the two correct sibling call sites (spawn_worker, spawn_subtree) in spawn.rs.
- DO NOT make this a silent behavior change for existing single-entry-allowlist projects (e.g. beast-rs's `roles.worker.allow = ["opencode"]"` with no catalog data at all) — if no catalog is configured, current fallback behavior (defer entirely to `.exo/config.toml`'s static per-role model) must be preserved exactly. Fail open to today's behavior, not to a guessed model id.

## OPEN DESIGN QUESTIONS TO RESOLVE BEFORE IMPLEMENTING (record the decision in a plan/decision comment on this issue)
1. Where does `ModelCatalog` data come from in a live run? Options: (a) a Rust effect that lists configured models per harness from `.exo/config.toml`/harness config, surfaced to Python via the existing EffectClient boundary (tl_loop/CLAUDE.md's RLM/effect pattern is the closest precedent); (b) a checked-in `.exo/model-catalog.json` the operator maintains, parallel to `harness_policy.toml`. (b) is far less invasive and matches this project's "human-authored allowlist" philosophy for harness_policy.toml — prefer it unless there's a reason live Rust-sourced data is required.
2. What's the difficulty→tier mapping unit? Likely: TRIVIAL/STANDARD → catalog's default/cheapest capable entry (today's behavior, unchanged); HARD, or `_failed_harness`-triggered escalation (attempts >= escalate_after_attempts with NO_GO), → catalog's strongest capable entry for that harness. Reuse `Difficulty`'s existing rank ordering (capability.py's `_DIFFICULTY_RANK`) rather than inventing a new scale.
3. Should model escalation piggyback on the *same* `escalate_after_attempts` threshold agent_type.py already uses for harness escalation, or a separate config knob? Prefer reusing the existing threshold first — a second independent counter is exactly the kind of duplicated authority this issue is about removing.

## STEPS (once design questions above are answered and recorded)
1. Extend `select_model`'s call site in driver.py (~3917-3921) to pass a computed `requested_model` derived from `classification.difficulty` and `slice_state.attempts`/`verdict`, instead of the current static `config.requested_model`. Keep `config.requested_model` as an explicit operator override that still wins (mirrors `effective_model_for`'s override-wins-over-config precedence on the Rust side — keep the two symmetric).
2. Wire `TLLoopConfig.catalog` from whatever source is chosen in design question 1, for real (non-test) runs — likely in whatever module constructs `TLLoopConfig` for `python3 -m tl_loop` / the TL window entrypoint.
3. Ensure the "unresolved" log line (driver.py:3956) only appears when a catalog genuinely has no entry for the harness (an operator-visible gap), not as the routine steady state it is today.
4. Update tl_loop/CLAUDE.md's "Selector budget ledger" section (or add a new section) documenting the difficulty→model mapping and where catalog data comes from, per this project's rule of always updating CLAUDE.md alongside behavior changes.

## READ FIRST
- tl_loop/select/classify.py (Difficulty, classify_task)
- tl_loop/select/agent_type.py:150-198 (existing difficulty/attempt-aware harness escalation — the pattern to mirror for models)
- tl_loop/select/model.py (select_model, ModelCatalog, CatalogModel)
- tl_loop/loop/driver.py:3890-3960 (the only call site)
- .exo/harness_policy.toml (human-authored boundary this must not widen)
- tl_loop/CLAUDE.md § "Learned dispatch policy" (existing precedent for a validated, human-boundary-respecting learned preference store — DispatchPolicyStore may be a better home for catalog data than a new mechanism; evaluate before adding a fourth config file)

## VERIFY
- tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tl_loop/tests   (must stay green; add tests for: HARD-classified slice resolves to strongest capable catalog entry; TRIVIAL/STANDARD unchanged; attempts >= escalate_after_attempts + NO_GO escalates model tier same as it escalates harness; no catalog configured → today's exact fallback behavior, unresolved log line included)
- tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m ruff check tl_loop
- Full E2E: exercise against beast-workspace or an equivalent fixture project with a real multi-tier catalog configured, confirm the dispatched agent actually receives the escalated model (depends on #913 being merged first).

## DONE CRITERIA
- Design questions above answered and recorded on this issue before implementation starts.
- select_model() receives a difficulty/attempt-derived reference in production runs when a catalog is configured, not just in tests.
- Behavior is unchanged (byte-for-byte) for any project with no catalog configured, including the "unresolved" log line semantics for that case.
- tl_loop/CLAUDE.md documents the new mapping.
- Full tl_loop test suite + ruff green.

RESEARCH POINTER (per operator request) — https://github.com/tkellogg/model-selection, a Claude Code skill that ranks models via Artificial Analysis's free benchmark API. It's built for a live interactive agent picking a model on demand, not a deterministic batch controller, so it does not port directly — but two pieces of it answer this issue's open design questions directly, and one constraint from this project rules out its core mechanism.

## WHY IT DOESN'T PORT AS-IS
The skill's `fetch`/`rank` commands make a live HTTP call to `artificialanalysis.ai` (24h disk cache, stale-fallback, 1,000 req/day free-tier ceiling, requires an API key in `creds.json`). tl_loop's selection layer cannot take on a live third-party network dependency or a secret in the hot dispatch path: `classify.py` is explicitly "deterministic, explainable task-difficulty classification," and `harness_policy.toml`/`capability.py` are human-authored, checked-in boundaries the selector "cannot widen" at runtime. A live external ranking call at dispatch time breaks both properties — determinism (API can change/rate-limit/go down mid-run) and the closed, auditable boundary the rest of `tl_loop/select/` is built on.

## WHAT DOES APPLY — answers to #914's open design questions

**Design question 1 (where does ModelCatalog data come from):** this resolves it in favor of option (b), the checked-in `.exo/model-catalog.json`, not a live Rust effect. Use a tool shaped like this skill's `rank` command *offline*, as an operator workflow — the human (or an operator-run agent, off the hot path) periodically runs a benchmark lookup and writes the resulting catalog file, the same way `harness_policy.toml` is hand-authored rather than computed live. The selector then only ever reads the static, checked-in file at dispatch time — zero network calls, zero new runtime secrets, same audit story as the rest of `.exo/`.

**Design question 2 (difficulty→tier mapping, avoid a hardcoded model-id table):** the skill's `topic_score()` (scripts/model_selection.py) is a reusable *shape*, not code to import: prefer a topic-level composite benchmark index when the catalog has one (e.g. a `coding_index`-style field, since tl_loop's leaves are exclusively coding tasks — narrower than the skill's general/writing/agents/math/etc. topic list), else average whatever raw per-benchmark fields are present. Its `cost_per_intelligence_point = price_per_1m_tokens / topic_score` (0-100 scale) is a clean, principled way to order catalog entries by cost-efficiency instead of an arbitrary hand-ranked list. Concretely, if `.exo/model-catalog.json` entries carry a `coding_score` and `price_per_1m_tokens` field (populated by whatever offline process produces the file — could literally be seeded from an Artificial Analysis pull, done once, by hand, not by the controller):
- TRIVIAL/STANDARD, first attempt → lowest `cost_per_intelligence_point` capable entry (today's "cheapest capable" behavior, now principled instead of arbitrary).
- HARD, or escalated via the existing `escalate_after_attempts` threshold → highest raw `coding_score` capable entry, cost-per-intelligence ignored (matches how harness escalation already trades cost for capability on repeated NO-GOs, agent_type.py:181-198).
This keeps the mapping catalog-driven (score/cost fields the operator can update by re-running an offline benchmark pull) rather than a vendor-specific model-id table baked into `tl_loop/select/`, per the existing anti-pattern in this issue's spec.

**Not in scope for #914, noted for later:** the skill's `discover` subcommand (reads Codex's `models_cache.json`/`config.toml` and Claude's `settings.json` to find out which model names/aliases are *actually invocable* in the current runtime, explicitly flagging Claude Code's inability to enumerate full account entitlement) has no analog in exomonad today — `.exo/model-catalog.json` and `.exo/config.toml`'s static model strings are both currently trusted blind, with no verification that a named model id is real or reachable. Worth its own future issue if catalog entries start silently referencing dead/renamed model ids; out of scope here.

DESIGN DECISION (recorded before implementation). Open design questions resolved:

1. Catalog source — option (b): checked-in `.exo/model-catalog.json`, human-authored offline (same audit story as harness_policy.toml). Missing file = fail open to today's behavior (catalog=None). Present-but-malformed file = fail closed (raise ModelResolutionError). No live Rust effect, no network call in the hot dispatch path.

2. Difficulty→tier mapping — catalog-driven, no vendor-specific model-id table. CatalogModel gains optional `coding_score` and `price_per_1m_tokens` fields (seeded offline, e.g. from an Artificial Analysis pull). `select_model_for_difficulty(harness, catalog, difficulty, escalated=...)`:
   - TRIVIAL/STANDARD, not escalated → lowest `price_per_1m_tokens / coding_score` (cost per intelligence point); records missing score/price are deprioritized to the end, ties resolve to catalog order (deterministic).
   - HARD, or escalated → highest raw `coding_score`.
   - No catalog entry for the harness → ModelResolutionError (operator-visible gap), not a silent guess.

3. Model escalation reuses the existing `escalate_after_attempts` threshold — driven by the same NO_GO + attempts signal the harness selector already computes, surfaced through `HarnessChoice.reason == "escalated_after_no_go"`. No second counter.

Precedence at the driver call site (mirrors effective_model_for's override-wins-over-config): `config.requested_model` (operator override) > difficulty/attempt-derived tier (when catalog present) > `route.model` harness-pin (no catalog). The "unresolved" log line remains only when no catalog AND no harness-pinned model.

REOPENED + FIXED the end-to-end gaps the review caught. (1) resume_pr now threads a model override: Python client resume_pr(model=...), _route_repair computes _repair_model(current, config) (strong catalog entry when attempts >= escalate_after_attempts), compose_repair/_dispatch_resume pass it, Haskell ResumePrArgs/ResumePrConfig carry rpcModel -> SpawnLeafSubtreeRequest.model, and the Rust resume_existing_pr handler sets SpawnLeafOptions.model instead of None. (2) model.py now rejects negative, out-of-range (>100), NaN, and infinite coding_score/price values (fail-closed catalog). Tests: _repair_model escalation, repair model reaching resume_pr, and validation cases. Verified: tl_loop pytest 443, ruff clean, wasm-guest tests 72, cargo test -p exomonad-core --lib 952.

SECOND REVIEW FIX — model precedence in repair dispatch. _repair_model now enforces the documented precedence (explicit requested_model > difficulty-derived tier > preserved current model): (1) requested_model is resolved against the catalog and returned for every repair regardless of attempt count; (2) below the escalation threshold the slice's current catalog-selected model is preserved instead of returning None (so a threshold > 1 no longer falls back to the Rust static default mid-repair); (3) at the threshold it escalates to the strongest catalog entry. Added tests: preserve-below-threshold, escalate-at-threshold, requested_model-wins-at-any-attempt, and no-catalog-preserves-current-model. tl_loop pytest 446, ruff clean.

THIRD REVIEW FIX — requested_model now requires a catalog. TLLoopConfig.__post_init__ rejects requested_model set without catalog (ValueError 'requested_model requires a model catalog'), so the initial-dispatch (resolve via select_model) and repair-dispatch (resolve via select_model) paths can no longer diverge. Added test_requested_model_requires_catalog. tl_loop pytest 447, ruff clean.

issues.title: spawn_leaf_subtree ignores SpawnLeafOptions.model, silently dropping any per-slice model override

comments.content:
WORKER SPEC — follow exactly. Context: subissue of #912 (see parent for full diagnosis).

## ROOT CAUSE
rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/spawn.rs:1790, inside `spawn_leaf_subtree_with_intent` (the function the `spawn_leaf` MCP tool actually calls — the TL's primary dev-leaf dispatch path):

    let model = self.effective_model_for(agent_type, role.as_str(), None);

The third argument is hardcoded `None` instead of `options.model.as_deref()`. `SpawnLeafOptions.model: Option<String>` (mod.rs:544-545) is documented as "Optional model override, separate from the agent type" and IS populated end-to-end from tl_loop's `client.spawn_leaf(model=selected_model)` call (driver.py `_leaf_call`, ~4002) through Haskell's `SpawnLeafArgs.slModel` (Spawn.hs) into `SpawnLeafOptions.model` — but it is silently discarded at the one place that should consume it.

Compare the two call sites that get this right:
- spawn.rs:1072 (`spawn_worker` path): `let model = self.effective_model_for(agent_type, role.as_str(), options.model.as_deref());`
- spawn.rs:1273 (`spawn_subtree` path): same pattern.

`effective_model_for` (mod.rs:911-929) already has correct precedence — override_model (if non-empty) wins over the static per-role config default — so this is a one-line consumption bug, not a design change.

## ANTI-PATTERNS (DO NOT)
- DO NOT touch `effective_model_for`'s precedence logic — it is already correct.
- DO NOT change spawn.rs:1072 or spawn.rs:1273 (spawn_worker, spawn_subtree) — they already thread the override correctly; this is scoped to the one broken call site.
- DO NOT change spawn.rs:669 or spawn.rs:1790's sibling context lines that intentionally pass `None` for a *different* reason (e.g. line 669 is inside the GitHub-issue auto-spawn path where there is no caller-supplied model at all) — verify with `git blame`/surrounding context which `None` is the actual bug before editing.
- DO NOT add a new config field or fallback chain — the existing `Option<String>` plumbing is sufficient once wired.

## READ FIRST
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/spawn.rs:1545-1600 (spawn_leaf_subtree / spawn_leaf_subtree_with_intent signature)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/spawn.rs:1780-1802 (the exact buggy block, `identity_model` construction that follows it)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/spawn.rs:1060-1080 (correct sibling: spawn_worker)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/spawn.rs:1265-1280 (correct sibling: spawn_subtree)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/mod.rs:534-560 (SpawnLeafOptions struct, model field)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/mod.rs:911-929 (effective_model_for)

## STEPS
1. In `spawn_leaf_subtree_with_intent`, change line 1790 from `self.effective_model_for(agent_type, role.as_str(), None)` to `self.effective_model_for(agent_type, role.as_str(), options.model.as_deref())`.
2. Check the `identity_model` chain immediately below (mod.rs:1792-1796) still behaves correctly now that `model` can be Some from an explicit override on a *fresh* spawn (not just from `existing_identity_record`/`prior_identity`) — it should, since it already falls back to `model.clone()` last, but confirm no test assumed `model` was always `None` on this path for fresh spawns.
3. Add a regression test in the spawn.rs test module (see existing tests near `test_find_existing_leaf_worktree_by_slug_uses_recorded_agent_type_suffix`, line ~2314, for the test harness pattern) asserting that a `spawn_leaf` call with `SpawnLeafOptions.model = Some("some/model-id")` results in the spawned agent's persisted identity/invocation record carrying that exact model id, not the static config default. Use two distinct values (config default vs. override) in the test fixture so the assertion can't pass by coincidence.
4. Do not change anything in tl_loop/ or Haskell for this subissue — `model` already reaches `SpawnLeafOptions` correctly; this is scoped to the single Rust consumption site.

## VERIFY
- cargo test -p exomonad-core agent_control::spawn -- --nocapture   (or the project's `just rust-test` equivalent scoped to this module)
- just rust-test    (full library-only loop, must stay green)
- Confirm via the new regression test that model=None still falls back to the static per-role config value (no regression to the common case).

## DONE CRITERIA
- spawn.rs:1790 threads `options.model.as_deref()` exactly like spawn_worker/spawn_subtree.
- New regression test proves an explicit `spawn_leaf` model override reaches the spawned agent's model field, and proves the None case still falls back to config as before.
- `just rust-test` green.
- Does not touch tl_loop/, Haskell, or the two correct sibling call sites.

REOPENED + FIXED the launch gap the review caught. The prior commit only recorded the model in identity/invocation metadata; the leaf CLI still launched via new_tmux_window (which passes None for the model override). Fixed: spawn_leaf_subtree_with_intent now calls new_tmux_window_inner directly with model.as_deref() and effort.as_deref() (plus role + claude_flags, matching spawn_subtree), so the resolved override actually reaches build_agent_command_with_effort and the CLI --model flag. Verified cargo test -p exomonad-core --lib (952) and clippy clean.

SECOND REVIEW FIX — launch-command regression coverage. Extracted build_launch_command (the pure command builder new_tmux_window_inner uses, resolving model/effort from the override or static per-role default) and added launch_command_threads_model_override_into_the_cli, which asserts an explicit override produces --model override-model and None falls back to --model config-default in the exact CLI command string. This covers the launch-command boundary the earlier fix crossed. cargo test -p exomonad-core --lib 953, clippy + fmt clean.

THIRD REVIEW FIX — regression now starts from SpawnLeafOptions.model. Extracted leaf_launch_command (resolves model/effort from options via effective_model_for/effective_effort_for, then builds the command) and new_tmux_window_with_command (tmux window creation), and spawn_leaf_subtree_with_intent now calls write_prompt_file -> leaf_launch_command -> new_tmux_window_with_command. The test leaf_launch_command_threads_spawn_leaf_options_model constructs a SpawnLeafOptions with model=Some("override-model") and asserts the command carries --model override-model; model=None falls back to --model config-default. Reverting either the effective_model_for args or the launch args would now fail the test. cargo test -p exomonad-core --lib 953, clippy + fmt clean.

issues.title: Per-slice model selection is architecturally dead: select_model() never wired, config.toml is the sole authority
issues.description:
Steps to reproduce:
1. 

Expected: 
Actual:

comments.content:
DIAGNOSIS — discovered live in beast-workspace/workspace while investigating why the TL dispatch log printed 'model=unresolved' for opencode leaves and why worker_model is unpinned in that project's config.toml.

## SUMMARY
There are three independent, disconnected mechanisms that all claim a piece of "which model runs this task," and none of them actually implements a task-difficulty/attempt-aware model choice end to end:

1. `tl_loop/select/agent_type.py` (`select_harness`) IS difficulty- and attempt-aware — `classify_task()` produces a `Difficulty`, and `_failed_harness()`/`_capable_harnesses()` escalate to a different *harness* after `role_policy.escalate_after_attempts` consecutive NO-GOs (agent_type.py:167-198). But this only ever chooses among bare agent types in `harness_policy.toml`'s `allow` list (e.g. `["opencode"]`, `["claude"]`) — it cannot pick a model *within* one harness. With a single-entry allowlist (the common case, e.g. beast-rs's `roles.worker.allow = ["opencode"]`), the escalation is a structural no-op: there is nothing to escalate to.

2. `tl_loop/select/model.py` (`select_model`) is the function that reads as "the model heuristic" — but it is dead code in every real run:
   - `TLLoopConfig.catalog: ModelCatalog | None = None` (driver.py:499) is never assigned outside the test suite — grep confirms zero non-test call sites set `.catalog`.
   - driver.py:3918 only calls `select_model(...)` `if config.catalog is not None`; since that's always false in production, it falls through to `model_id = route.model`, which is `None` for a bare harness string like `"opencode"` (no `/model` suffix — and `harness_policy.toml`'s own header comment says entries must stay bare agent types). The dispatch log then prints `model_id or "unresolved"` (driver.py:3956) — that's the literal source of the "unresolved" log line.
   - Even if a catalog *were* wired, `select_model(harness, catalog, requested_model, *, provider_default=None, exact_reference=False)` has no difficulty or attempt-count parameter at all. It can only resolve an already-known model *reference* string against a catalog (exact match → alias → dated → provider_default → fallback-to-first-record). Nothing computes "this slice is HARD / on attempt 3, so ask for a stronger model" and turns it into that `requested_model` argument. The difficulty signal that (1) computes is never handed to (2).

3. The model that actually runs is a single project-wide static string: `.exo/config.toml`'s `[opencode].worker_model`/`tl_model` (or Claude/Codex effort flags), resolved once per role in Rust (`rust/exomonad/src/config.rs`, threaded via `AgentControlService::effective_model_for` in `rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/mod.rs:911-929`). This has zero per-slice, per-difficulty, or per-attempt parameterization — it is exactly the "operator judgment for the default low-cost worker model" the scaffold comment (`rust/exomonad/src/new.rs:12`) says it is, nothing more. This is why beast-rs's `.exo/config.toml` has no `[opencode]` section at all today: there was never a live per-task heuristic to defer to, so pinning (or not pinning) a static model is the *only* lever that currently does anything.

## CONCRETE PLUMBING BUG (not just an architecture gap)
`effective_model_for(agent_type, role, override_model)` (mod.rs:911-929) DOES already implement the right precedence — an explicit per-call override wins over the static config pin. And `SpawnLeafOptions.model: Option<String>` (mod.rs:544-545, "Optional model override, separate from the agent type") exists and IS threaded from tl_loop's `spawn_leaf(model=selected_model)` call through Haskell (`slModel` in `SpawnLeafArgs`, Spawn.hs) down to Rust.
But `spawn_leaf_subtree_with_intent` — the function `spawn_leaf` actually calls, i.e. the TL's primary dev-leaf dispatch path — never reads it:

    rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/spawn.rs:1790
    let model = self.effective_model_for(agent_type, role.as_str(), None);   // <- hardcoded None

Compare `spawn_worker` (spawn.rs:1072) and `spawn_subtree` (spawn.rs:1273), which both correctly pass `options.model.as_deref()`. So even after fixing (1)+(2) to compute a real difficulty-aware model choice per slice, that value would be silently dropped for every `spawn_leaf` dispatch — the single most common path — until this line is fixed too.

## WHY THIS MATTERS
The user's framing is correct: `.exo/config.toml` pinning a model at the project level should be the *fallback*, not the *only* live mechanism, if `select_model()`'s catalog+heuristic machinery is meant to actually run. Right now it's dead weight — code that reads as authoritative in `tl_loop/select/model.py` and is documented as such in `tl_loop/CLAUDE.md`, but contributes nothing to any real dispatch decision, while a completely separate, non-difficulty-aware static config value is what actually governs model choice.

## SPLIT INTO TWO SUBISSUES
- Subissue A (mechanical, testable, do first): fix spawn.rs:1790 to thread `options.model` through, matching spawn_worker/spawn_subtree. Cheap, low-risk, and a prerequisite for B to matter at all.
- Subissue B (design + implementation): decide how `classify_task()`'s `Difficulty` and `slice.attempts`/`verdict` history should map to a `requested_model` reference, wire a real `ModelCatalog` into `TLLoopConfig.catalog` for production runs (not just tests), and make `select_model()` receive that computed reference instead of always falling through to `route.model`.

## READ FIRST
- tl_loop/select/agent_type.py (select_harness, classify_task usage, escalation)
- tl_loop/select/model.py (select_model, ModelCatalog)
- tl_loop/loop/driver.py:3890-3960 (dispatch, model_id resolution, logging)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/mod.rs:911-929 (effective_model_for)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/spawn.rs:1060-1080, 1270-1280, 1786-1796 (the three model-threading call sites, only one of which is wrong)
- .exo/harness_policy.toml (harness_policy.toml's own comment on why models are NOT allowed there)

issues.title: Fix TL controller crash loop when CI failure arrives before any review

comments.content:
WORKER SPEC — follow exactly. Prior context: discovered live in beast-workspace/workspace (PR #42, slice 'tunable-operator-body'): crash loop after rebuild; the #910 identity fix works (event now resolves to the slice), but the controller dies one step later inside _route_ci_event.

## ROOT CAUSE
tl_loop/loop/driver.py:4453-4459 (_route_ci_event):
    updated[slice_id] = replace(
        current,
        pr_number=event.pr_number or current.pr_number,
        ci_state=ci_state,
        verdict=Verdict.NO_GO if status == "failure" else current.verdict,
        verdict_at=event.observed_at if status == "failure" else current.verdict_at,
    )
A ci.status_changed failure event unconditionally stamps verdict=NO_GO. If no review has landed yet (reviewed_head=None — e.g. watcher reports PendingReview, or review races CI), the subsequent store.checkpoint() fails the schema invariant 'reviewed_head is required when verdict is present' (tl_loop/state/schema.py:694-697) and raises. Because the checkpoint write is what raised, the ledger cursor never advances: every restart replays the same event and crashes identically (permanent crash loop until the ledger event is manually purged).

Note the repair branch directly below (driver.py:4461-4467) already gates on current.reviewed_head == head_sha — the verdict write just was never guarded the same way.

## ANTI-PATTERNS (DO NOT)
- DO NOT drop or quarantine the CI event — ci_state MUST still be recorded for the head unconditionally; review-then-CI ordering must not lose CI evidence.
- DO NOT relax the schema invariant in schema.py (reviewed_head required with verdict) — it is correct; the writer is wrong.
- DO NOT set verdict_at without verdict or vice versa; keep them as an atomic pair.
- DO NOT convert the crash into a swallowed exception around store.checkpoint — fix the state written, not the validation.
- DO NOT change _route_review_event/pr.review handling — only the CI path is affected.

## FIX
In _route_ci_event only set the verdict pair when review evidence exists for the observed head:
    has_review_for_head = current.reviewed_head == head_sha
    updated[slice_id] = replace(
        current,
        pr_number=event.pr_number or current.pr_number,
        ci_state=ci_state,
        verdict=(Verdict.NO_GO if status == "failure" else current.verdict) if has_review_for_head else current.verdict,
        verdict_at=(event.observed_at if status == "failure" else current.verdict_at) if has_review_for_head else current.verdict_at,
    )
Rationale: a verdict adjudicates a reviewed head; without review there is no head to adjudicate. ci_state accumulation alone preserves the failure evidence — the slice stays IN_REVIEW/SPAWNED and reconciliation (_apply_reconciliation_observations, driver.py:1863-1873) or a later pr.review event supplies reviewed_head+verdict.

## READ FIRST
- tl_loop/loop/driver.py:4430-4500 (_route_ci_event and repair branch)
- tl_loop/state/schema.py:675-707 (_validate_slice invariant)
- tl_loop/tests/test_driver.py:1226-1264 (test_ci_failure_records_head_and_resumes_same_pr — existing reviewed_head='head-a' fixture), 1368 (_ci_failure_event)
- tl_loop/loop/driver.py:1841-1878 (_apply_reconciliation_observations — how recovery supplies verdict when review exists)

## TESTS TO ADD (tl_loop/tests/test_driver.py)
1. test_ci_failure_before_review_records_ci_state_without_verdict (THE regression test, must fail pre-fix):
   store = _review_store(tmp_path) with reviewed_head=None, verdict=None passed through _review_store's kwargs (extend the helper or build inline like the existing fixture at test_driver.py:1273-1305, SliceState(... reviewed_head=None, verdict=None)).
   Call _route_ci_event(store, store.load(), TLPlanning(), _ci_failure_event(), 1, TLLoopConfig(active=True), EffectClient(RecordingTransport()), []).
   Assert: no exception; reloaded slice has ci_state == {'head-a': 'failure'}; verdict is None; verdict_at is None; status is still IN_REVIEW.
2. Keep test_ci_failure_records_head_and_resumes_same_pr green (reviewed_head='head-a' + verdict=GO fixture → still NO_GO + REPAIRING + resume_pr).
3. test_ci_failure_after_review_but_different_head_does_not_overwrite_verdict: fixture reviewed_head='head-b', verdict=GO; event head_sha='head-a' failure → verdict stays GO, ci_state gains 'head-a'.

## VERIFY
- cd tl_loop && ../tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/test_driver.py -k ci   (or from repo root: tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tl_loop/tests/test_driver.py)
- Full suite: tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tl_loop/tests  (420 tests currently — must stay green, +3 new)
- Lint: tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m ruff check tl_loop tests/e2e
- Prove the regression test fails pre-fix: git stash the driver.py change (keep the test), run test 1, confirm it raises the schema error, then unstash.

## DONE CRITERIA
- CI failure before review: no crash, ci_state recorded, verdict stays None, slice remains reviewable.
- CI failure after review on matching head: unchanged behavior (NO_GO, repair path, resume_pr).
- Full suite + ruff green; regression test proven to fail against pre-fix code.
- This unblocks the beast-workspace PR #42 crash loop on next rebuild+init (no ledger surgery needed).

Fixed in commit 34689190: gated CI-failure verdict/verdict_at on current.reviewed_head == head_sha; ci_state still records unconditionally. 3 new regression tests added (incl. the exact crash shape: CI failure before review), full suite 423 passed, ruff clean, git-stash proof confirms all 3 fail pre-fix with the exact schema error from the ticket.

issues.title: Fix reviewer loss on crash between reviewer-attempt claim checkpoint and reviewer spawn

comments.content:
Crash window found during review of #903–#908 fixes (round 2 verification).

**Location:** tl_loop/loop/driver.py — reconciliation path ~1770-1775 (_reconcile_nonterminal_slices: pending_reviewer_spawns loop) and live event path ~1087-1110 (claim → checkpoint → _spawn_reviewer_for_head).

**Problem:** Both paths durably checkpoint the reviewer_attempt claim ({head_sha: 1}) BEFORE invoking spawn_reviewer. If the process dies in between, restart reconciliation sees reviewer_attempt[head_sha] > 0, treats the head as already claimed, and skips spawning — the PR is never reviewed and the reviewer is permanently lost until manual intervention.

**Scope:** Inherited property of the system's current guarantee level, not a regression from the #903–#908 round — the reconciliation path deliberately mirrors the live event path's ordering.

**Possible directions (to be decided by implementer):**
- Spawn before claim + rely on spawn idempotency/journal to deduplicate on retry, or
- Distinguish 'claimed but spawn not confirmed' (e.g. persist intent/journal entry first, treat unconfirmed spawn as retryable like the action journal's intended/unknown pattern), or
- Track spawn confirmation separately from the attempt claim so reconciliation can re-spawn unconfirmed attempts.

**Existing tests to keep green:** tl_loop/tests/test_startup_reconciliation.py (test_reconciliation_does_not_respawn_reviewer_when_head_already_claimed, test_reconciliation_recovers_and_persists_missing_pr_number), tests/e2e/init-recovery/run.sh Phase 7.

WORKER SPEC — follow exactly. (Supersedes the 'possible directions' note above; investigation since then found a preferred design.)

## ROOT CAUSE (both paths)
Live event path (tl_loop/loop/driver.py:1085-1110) and reconciliation path (driver.py:1750-1775, _reconcile_nonterminal_slices) both durably checkpoint the reviewer_attempt claim {head_sha: 1} BEFORE spawn_reviewer is dispatched. On restart, reconciliation's spawn guard requires reconciled.reviewer_attempt.get(head_sha, 0) == 0 — a claim persisted before a crash in that window looks identical to a completed spawn, so the reviewer is never spawned and the PR is never reviewed (silent stall, not a crash).

Key enabling fact already in the codebase: spawn_reviewer goes through _invoke (driver.py:4714-4774) and is in MUTATING_OPERATIONS (tl_loop/loop/journal.py:17), so the EffectJournal already records the spawn as intended→confirmed and _invoke REPLAYS a confirmed entry instead of re-dispatching. The durable record of 'did the spawn actually happen' already exists — reconciliation just doesn't consult it.

## ANTI-PATTERNS (DO NOT)
- DO NOT spawn BEFORE the claim checkpoint — that inverts the bug (crash after spawn but before claim → duplicate reviewer on restart).
- DO NOT remove the reviewer_attempt claim or change its schema shape {head_sha: int}.
- DO NOT relax _invoke's journal semantics (intended/unknown blocking, confirmed replay) — build on them.
- DO NOT break the two existing guard tests: test_reconciliation_does_not_respawn_reviewer_when_head_already_claimed and test_reconciliation_recovers_and_persists_missing_pr_number (tl_loop/tests/test_startup_reconciliation.py). The first constructs a 'claimed' state with NO journal evidence and asserts no spawn — see STEPS for how both stay true.
- DO NOT change the live event path's ordering in this issue unless the chosen design requires it for symmetry; keep scope minimal.

## PREFERRED DESIGN
In _reconcile_nonterminal_slices, treat a claimed attempt as spawn-proven ONLY when the action journal confirms it:
- New helper, e.g. _reviewer_spawn_confirmed(effects_log, slice_id, pr_number, head_sha) -> bool | None:
  - If effects_log is not an EffectJournal (plain list — unit tests), return None = 'unknown, assume claimed means spawned' (preserves test_reconciliation_does_not_respawn_reviewer_when_head_already_claimed unchanged).
  - If it IS an EffectJournal: return True iff a journal entry exists with operation='spawn_reviewer', target=slice_id, and status='confirmed', whose arguments' pr_number/head_sha match (arguments dict keys: pr_number, head_sha — see _spawn_reviewer_for_slice, driver.py:4982-4988).
- Spawn guard becomes: head not claimed (as today) OR (claimed AND _reviewer_spawn_confirmed(...) is False). 'False' = journal present and no confirmed entry → the claim was checkpointed but the spawn never landed (or died unknown) → re-attempt via _spawn_reviewer_for_slice; journal idempotency makes a retry safe (confirmed→replay, unknown→blocks behind the #905 gate as designed).
- Comment the crash window explicitly at the guard.

## READ FIRST
- tl_loop/loop/driver.py:1691-1780 (_reconcile_nonterminal_slices), 4966-5008 (_spawn_reviewer_for_slice), 4714-4774 (_invoke journal semantics)
- tl_loop/loop/journal.py (EffectJournal: existing(), append(), MUTATING_OPERATIONS, stable_action_key — spawn args must match exactly for a lookup; prefer scanning _read() entries by operation+target+status rather than recomputing keys)
- tl_loop/tests/test_startup_reconciliation.py (fixtures: _load_state, FakeClient; note effects_log arg is currently [] in these tests)
- tl_loop/tests/test_action_journal_reconciliation.py (how tests build a real EffectJournal in tmp_path)

## STEPS
1. Read the files above; run the reconciliation tests to confirm green baseline.
2. Implement _reviewer_spawn_confirmed + the new guard in _reconcile_nonterminal_slices.
3. Add tests (see below).
4. Run VERIFY.

## TESTS TO ADD (tl_loop/tests/test_startup_reconciliation.py)
Build a real EffectJournal in tmp_path (pattern: test_action_journal_reconciliation.py) and pass it as effects_log.
1. test_reconciliation_respawns_reviewer_when_claim_was_checkpointed_but_spawn_never_journaled (THE regression test, must fail pre-fix): slice with pr_number already recovered/persisted (fixture like test_reconciliation_recovers_and_persists_missing_pr_number) and reviewer_attempt={'head-a': 1} pre-claimed; effects_log = empty EffectJournal → assert client.spawn_reviewer_calls has exactly one call for head-a.
2. test_reconciliation_does_not_respawn_when_journal_confirms_the_spawn: same, but append+mark_result a spawn_reviewer intent (target=slice id, arguments pr_number/head matching) in the journal first → assert no spawn call.
3. test_reconciliation_keeps_assuming_claimed_means_spawned_without_a_journal: claimed state + plain list effects_log (no journal) → assert no spawn call (documents the conservative fallback).

## VERIFY
- tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tl_loop/tests/test_startup_reconciliation.py tl_loop/tests/test_action_journal_reconciliation.py
- Full suite: tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tl_loop/tests (currently 420 passing; must stay green +3)
- Lint: tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m ruff check tl_loop tests/e2e
- Prove test 1 fails pre-fix via git stash of the driver change.

## DONE CRITERIA
- A crash between the claim checkpoint and the spawn dispatch no longer permanently loses the reviewer: next reconciliation re-attempts (journal-safe).
- A genuinely spawned reviewer is never re-spawned (journal-confirmed short-circuit; no-journal fallback stays conservative).
- All existing reconciliation/journal tests green, 3 new tests, ruff clean, pre-fix failure proven.

Fixed in commit 1e4e5212: added EffectJournal.confirmed_entries() and _reviewer_spawn_confirmed(), so reconciliation's reviewer-spawn guard consults the action journal (scanned by operation/target/status, not a recomputed key) instead of assuming a checkpointed claim means a completed spawn. No-journal callers (plain-list effects_log) keep the original conservative fallback. 3 new tests added, full suite 426 passed, ruff clean (tl_loop + tests/e2e), git-stash proof confirms the regression test fails pre-fix while the other two pass trivially (matching the old bug's behavior).

issues.title: Make managed recursive routing E2E cleanup exception-safe
issues.description:
## ANTI-PATTERNS

- Do not start or restart exomonad init, exomonad serve, or exomonad new from tests or implementation sessions.
- Do not rely on outer tmux-session cleanup for the multiprocessing controller; it runs outside tmux.
- Do not raise from cleanup before every owned process and pane has received best-effort disposal.
- Do not silently ignore controller death or report only a generic timeout.
- Do not weaken the existing canonical CI identity, durable checkpoint, or exactly-once reviewer assertions.

## READ FIRST

- AGENTS.md
- tests/e2e/ordered-recursive/real_server_transport.py, especially assert_controller_alive, stop_spawned_worker, and run_real_watcher_routing_probe
- tests/e2e/ordered-recursive/run.sh and the managed E2E entrypoint
- tl_loop/loop/driver.py controller-exit and terminal-summary persistence paths
- Chainlink issue #901 and parent epic #898

## STEPS

1. Refactor run_real_watcher_routing_probe so all work after root_process.start is enclosed by exception-safe cleanup.
2. Track every spawned owner and reviewer identity as soon as it becomes known, and dispose each identity in a best-effort finally block.
3. Add a controller shutdown helper that performs terminate, bounded join, kill fallback, and final join; surface a precise error only after cleanup has converged.
4. Enhance controller-death and timeout errors with phase, exit code, checkpoint path and cursor/state when available, and recent matching ledger/controller-exit evidence.
5. Add deterministic regressions that inject failures during dispatch, PR publication, watcher delivery, checkpoint persistence, and reviewer stabilization, asserting no controller process or worker pane remains.
6. Preserve assertions for canonical CI owner_id, slice_id, branch, head_sha, status, durable review/CI consumption, and exactly-once reviewer spawning.
7. Run the managed live E2E three consecutive times once the harness cleanup tests pass; record the commands and outcomes on this issue.

## VERIFY

- cargo fmt --all --check
- cargo clippy -p exomonad-core --all-targets -- -D warnings
- cargo test -p exomonad-core --lib
- tl_loop/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -q tl_loop/tests

- Run the focused failure-injection cleanup regressions.
- Run the managed ordered-recursive E2E three consecutive times without leaked processes, panes, or stale checkpoints.

## DONE CRITERIA

- Every exit path after controller startup cleans up the controller and all probe-owned panes.
- A controller that ignores terminate is killed and reaped within a bounded interval.
- Failed probes produce actionable lifecycle, checkpoint, and ledger diagnostics.
- Failure-injection tests prove cleanup for each major probe phase.
- Existing routing, provenance, durable-state, and exactly-once assertions remain intact.
- Three consecutive managed live E2E runs pass.
- #901 may close only after this subissue is merged, verified, and its live-run evidence is recorded.

issues.title: Prove automatic recovery with lifecycle crash-injection E2E tests
issues.description:
## ANTI-PATTERNS
- Do not mock away the Rust watcher to ledger to Python controller boundary.
- Do not validate only that a process stayed alive; validate lifecycle state and side-effect cardinality.
- Do not use sleeps as the primary synchronization mechanism.
- Do not run destructive recovery tests in the developer workspace.

## READ FIRST
- tests/e2e/ordered-recursive and real_server_transport.py

- Plain init recovers every injected interruption without --recreate or manual checkpoint edits.
- Root and recursive orchestration converge deterministically.
- Each external side effect occurs exactly once.
- Failed tests retain complete, bounded recovery evidence and clean up disposable resources.
