issues.title: Session-start failsafe: fail loudly when CHAINLINK_DB is unset or points at a phantom DB
issues.description:
## Problem

#245 unified the canonical CHAINLINK_DB path and documented its propagation contract across all five agent runtimes. The remaining risk: if propagation ever silently breaks (env not inherited, tmux env stripped by a wrapper, a refactor regresses build_agent_command), an agent will run `chainlink ...` against the worktree's CWD, fail to find a DB, and chainlink will auto-create an empty one. Work then proceeds against a phantom DB that diverges from the canonical tracker.

The symptom is silent and late-discovered, exactly the class of failure the propagation contract was designed to prevent. We need an audible tripwire at session start so a missing env var triggers a hard stop, not a phantom DB.

## Anti-patterns (FIRST)
- DO NOT add the check in Rust. All hooks and tool logic live in Haskell WASM per CLAUDE.md § "All Tools and Hooks in Haskell WASM".
- DO NOT auto-fix by setting CHAINLINK_DB from inside the hook. The point is to surface the propagation failure, not paper over it.
- DO NOT log a warning and continue. The whole class of bug this prevents is silent divergence; a warning that gets swallowed in scrollback is functionally the same as no check.
- DO NOT scope this to one runtime. The check must fire on session start for Claude, Codex, Gemini, OpenCode, and worker panes alike. Each runtime's session-start hook entry point must invoke the same validation.
- DO NOT exempt the root TL. The root also runs chainlink commands; if its env is missing, surface it just as loudly.
- DO NOT validate by running `chainlink ping` or similar — keep the check filesystem-only so it works without the chainlink binary on PATH.

## Read first
- haskell/wasm-guest/src/ExoMonad/Guest/Tools/ — existing tool definitions for shape reference
- .exo/roles/devswarm/Main.hs — FFI exports including handle_session_start
- .exo/roles/devswarm/RootRole.hs, TLRole.hs, DevRole.hs, WorkerRole.hs — per-role hook config (the TL-edit guard from #234 is the closest precedent for a per-role hook deny pattern)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/internal.rs:131-152 — the CHAINLINK_DB propagation contract this hook defends
- rust/exomonad/src/init.rs:702-711 — the fallback tmux-env setter
- CODEX_HOOK_TRUST_INVESTIGATION.md and the closure comments on #233/#234/#235 — example of how recent hook work was structured

## Steps
1. Add a sessionStartCheckEnv (or similar) handler in the shared role module that runs at SessionStart for every role:
   - Read CHAINLINK_DB from the agent's process env via the existing env-read effect (or add one if missing).
   - If unset → emit a hook output that aborts session start with a clear error: "CHAINLINK_DB not set. ExoMonad spawn env is broken; refusing to start agent. Investigate build_agent_command in services/agent_control/internal.rs."
   - If set but the path does not exist on disk → emit a similar abort with the path included.
   - If set and the path exists but does not contain issues.db → emit a similar abort. (This catches "the directory got created empty by some other process" — phantom case.)
2. Wire the check into every per-role hook config (RootRole, TLRole, DevRole, WorkerRole, ReviewerRole). Each role's SessionStart handler should call the shared check first, before any role-specific logic.
3. Surface failures via the hook's stdout/exit_code so the spawned agent's runtime treats the session as un-started. For Claude that means SessionStart's stderr text is shown in the conversation. For Codex/Gemini/OpenCode, confirm the equivalent runtime behavior — if any runtime ignores SessionStart failures, fall back to a PreToolUse blanket-deny that fires on every tool call with the same error until env is fixed.
4. Add unit tests in the WASM guest tests for the three cases (unset / missing dir / dir without issues.db) using the existing pure-test pattern in haskell/wasm-guest/.
5. Add an E2E test under tests/e2e/chainlink-env-failsafe/ that spawns a leaf with CHAINLINK_DB explicitly stripped, asserts the agent fails to start (or fails on first tool call) with the canonical message.
6. Update CHAINLINK_PARALLEL_TIMERS_PLAN.md or write a short addendum doc explaining the layered defense: env propagation at spawn (covered by #245) plus session-start tripwire (this issue).

## Verify
- cabal test all (Haskell unit tests for the three failure cases)
- just test-fast — Rust unit tests still pass
- just check-fmt and just haskell-fmt clean
- Manual: in a session, spawn a leaf, temporarily strip CHAINLINK_DB from its env before runtime start, confirm the agent aborts with the canonical message
- Manual: spawn each runtime (Claude, Codex, Gemini, OpenCode, worker) with the env intentionally missing, confirm uniform failure behavior

## Done criteria
- An agent of any runtime that starts without CHAINLINK_DB set, or with it pointing at a non-existent directory, or at a directory without issues.db, aborts loudly with a clear canonical error message
- The check lives entirely in Haskell WASM; Rust contributes no new logic, only effect plumbing if a new env-read effect is needed
- Unit tests cover the three failure cases per role
- An E2E test reproduces the failure path end-to-end for at least one runtime
- Docs explain the two-layer defense (propagation at spawn + tripwire at session start)

## Why
#245 made the propagation contract correct and documented. This issue makes the contract self-defending. The combined effect: any future regression that breaks propagation surfaces as a loud session-start failure on the next spawn, instead of a silent phantom-DB divergence that takes a human days to notice. Cheap to add, expensive to omit.

issues.title: Verify and document CHAINLINK_DB propagation to spawned dev-leafs/workers across all agent types
issues.description:
## Problem

Dev-leaves run in git worktrees at .exo/worktrees/{slug}-{type}/, which contain no .chainlink/ directory. If a leaf invokes `chainlink issue show 123` from inside its worktree without CHAINLINK_DB set in its process env, chainlink will look in the worktree's CWD, not find the DB, and either fail or auto-create an empty one — silently divorcing the leaf from the canonical issue tracker.

Today CHAINLINK_DB IS set in two places:
1. rust/exomonad/src/init.rs:702-709 — set to `{cwd}/.chainlink/issues.db` (file path)
2. rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/internal.rs:132-139 — set to `{project_dir}/.chainlink` (directory path)

Two real issues:
- **Path-format inconsistency.** One site sets the file path, the other sets the directory. The chainlink CLI accepts both per its --db help text, but the inconsistency is a code-smell that becomes a bug the moment any downstream code (now or future) expects one specific form.
- **Propagation is not audited across all agent runtimes.** The env_vars HashMap returned by build_spawn_env() only reaches the child process if the agent's spawn path actually injects it. Claude (via tmux + .mcp.json env), Codex (.codex/config.toml or process env), Gemini (GEMINI_CLI_SYSTEM_SETTINGS_PATH or process env), OpenCode (TypeScript plugin env), and worker panes (tmux pane env) all have different propagation paths — we haven't confirmed CHAINLINK_DB reaches all of them.

The symptom is silent: a leaf that thinks it's tracking issues but is writing to a phantom DB. By the time anyone notices, work has diverged from chainlink's truth.

## Anti-patterns (FIRST)
- DO NOT trust that setting the env var in the HashMap reaches the child. Verify per agent type.
- DO NOT fix the inconsistency by leaving both formats and "trusting the CLI to handle both". Pick the directory form (matches the --help wording "Path to .chainlink directory or issues.db file" — the directory is the canonical resource, the file is an artifact inside it) and use it everywhere.
- DO NOT add a fallback that walks up parent dirs from the worktree to find .chainlink. Explicit env var is the contract; implicit discovery hides bugs.
- DO NOT change the canonical DB location. Leaves and workers must use the parent project's .chainlink/issues.db, not their worktree's.

## Read first
- rust/exomonad/src/init.rs:700-710 — init-time CHAINLINK_DB setup
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/internal.rs:115-148 — build_spawn_env (the HashMap)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/internal.rs — every spawn path: search for build_spawn_env callers, follow each to where it composes the actual child process Command. Confirm env_vars are merged into the Command's env.
- rust/exomonad-core/src/codex_config.rs — codex agent spawn (verify .codex/config.toml or process env carries CHAINLINK_DB)
- .exo/opencode-plugin/ — opencode hook bridge (does it inherit env from the parent process?)
- .exo/roles/devswarm/context/*.md — role context files; check whether they reference CHAINLINK_DB or assume leaves can run chainlink without it

## Steps
1. **Pick the canonical form**: directory path. Update init.rs:702-709 to set CHAINLINK_DB = `{cwd}/.chainlink` (no `/issues.db` suffix). internal.rs:132-139 is already correct.
2. **Audit propagation per agent type.** For each of (Claude, Codex, Gemini, OpenCode, worker-pane), trace from build_spawn_env to the child process invocation and confirm:
   - The HashMap entry CHAINLINK_DB is added to the Command's env, OR
   - A config file written by exomonad explicitly carries the value into the agent's runtime
   Write the audit as inline doc-comments on each spawn site so future readers see the propagation contract.
3. **Add a regression test per agent type** that spawns a fake agent runtime (a shell that just prints its env) and asserts CHAINLINK_DB appears in the child env with the expected directory-form path.
4. **Document in role context.** Add a one-paragraph note to .exo/roles/devswarm/context/dev.md and worker.md (or wherever the agent-facing role rules live) telling leaves: "You are in a git worktree. The canonical chainlink DB is at $CHAINLINK_DB — exomonad sets this env var for you. Use `chainlink ...` commands normally; they will hit the right DB. Do NOT use the --db flag explicitly unless overriding for testing."
5. **Add a smoke check at session start.** When a dev-leaf or worker starts up (likely a hook), assert CHAINLINK_DB is set and points to an existing directory containing issues.db. If not, fail loudly with a clear message rather than letting chainlink auto-create a phantom DB.

## Verify
- cargo test --workspace — existing tests pass plus the new propagation tests
- Manual: spawn a Claude leaf, verify `echo $CHAINLINK_DB` in its tmux window prints `{project_dir}/.chainlink`
- Manual: same for Codex, Gemini, OpenCode, and a worker pane
- Manual: in a leaf's worktree, run `chainlink issue list` — confirm it returns the parent project's issues, not an empty/phantom list
- Manual: temporarily unset CHAINLINK_DB in a leaf, run a chainlink command, confirm the session-start hook caught it and refused to proceed

## Done criteria
- CHAINLINK_DB is set to the same directory-form value at every site
- Every agent runtime's spawn path has an inline comment explaining how the env var reaches the child
- Regression tests assert CHAINLINK_DB propagation for all five agent types (claude, codex, gemini, opencode, worker-pane)
- Role context docs tell leaves where the canonical DB lives and that they do not need to think about it
- A leaf that somehow loses CHAINLINK_DB at runtime fails loudly instead of silently creating a phantom DB

## Why
The session-state divergence this prevents is a class of bug we cannot afford. "The worker thinks it tracked the work but the TL sees nothing" is the worst kind of orchestration failure — silent, late-discovered, and erodes trust in the whole tracker. issues.title: chainlink source: support concurrent timers (one per issue) — TL cannot parallel-delegate today
issues.description:
## Problem

The chainlink CLI today enforces "exactly one active timer at a time" globally. Code is at /home/goya/agent-workspace/chainlink/chainlink/src/commands/timer.rs:7-45 and the underlying db method is db.get_active_timer() -> Option<(issue_id, started_at)> — singular by type. `timer start` errors or auto-stops the previous timer; `timer stop` takes no ID; `timer show` returns a single record.

This breaks exomonad's TL orchestration model. A TL that spawns N parallel leaves needs N concurrent timers (one per delegated issue), so it can:
- Track time-on-task per issue independently
- Stop the right timer when a specific PR merges, without disturbing siblings still in flight
- Surface "these issues have been open for X minutes" via `timer show` / `timer list` for stuck-detection

With the singleton model the TL is forced to pick one issue to time, defeating the entire point of parallel delegation. Per root.md § Chainlink Coordination, the TL is supposed to `chainlink_timer_start` when spawning and `chainlink_timer_stop` after merge — that's not possible when more than one child is in flight.

This is upstream work in the chainlink source repo (/home/goya/agent-workspace/chainlink), not in exomonad.

## Anti-patterns (FIRST)
- DO NOT preserve the singleton invariant with a "current timer" pointer alongside multiple stored timers. That creates two notions of "active" (current vs all-active) and invites the same bugs. Drop the singleton concept entirely.
- DO NOT auto-stop other timers when a new one starts. That's the current footgun. Concurrent timers must coexist.
- DO NOT default `timer stop` (no ID) to "the most recently started" or "the only active one". Ambiguous semantics → wrong-timer-stopped bugs. Require an explicit issue ID, OR provide a "stop all" flag.
- DO NOT change the public DB file location (.chainlink/issues.db) or the table name in a non-additive way that breaks existing consumers (notably exomonad MCP tools).
- DO NOT skip a schema migration. Existing DBs in the wild must keep working.

## Read first
- /home/goya/agent-workspace/chainlink/chainlink/src/commands/timer.rs — entire file (start at lines 7, 40, 74)
- /home/goya/agent-workspace/chainlink/chainlink/src/db/*.rs — find the timer table definition and the get_active_timer method (likely in db/timers.rs or db/mod.rs). The schema is what defines the singleton invariant.
- Any existing migrations file/dir — model the new migration after the pattern already in use
- /home/goya/agent-workspace/exomonad/.exo/roles/devswarm/context/root.md § Chainlink Coordination — the TL behavior this unblocks (so the change targets the right surface)

## Steps
1. **Schema migration**: alter the timers table so multiple rows with stopped_at IS NULL can coexist. Likely no schema change is needed at the DB level (if rows already have a stopped_at column) — the singleton is enforced in code, not by a UNIQUE constraint. Verify either way and migrate if needed.
2. **DB layer**: replace get_active_timer() -> Option<(i64, DateTime)> with get_active_timers() -> Vec<(i64, DateTime)>. Keep the singular for backwards compat if other code depends on it, but the new code path uses the plural.
3. **`timer start <ID>`**: remove the "error or auto-stop the previous active timer" branch at commands/timer.rs:15. Allow starting if no timer is active FOR THAT ISSUE. Error if a timer for this same issue is already running (no double-start).
4. **`timer stop`**: accept an issue ID argument. `timer stop <ID>` stops the timer for that issue. Make the ID required (no implicit "current"). Add an explicit --all flag for stopping every active timer at once.
5. **`timer show`**: print all active timers as a table (issue ID, started_at, elapsed). Add `timer show <ID>` to show one specific issue's timer. Add `timer list` as an alias for `timer show` with no args, for discoverability.
6. **Idempotency**: `timer start` on an issue with an already-running timer is a clear error (not a silent no-op, not an auto-restart). `timer stop` on an issue with no active timer is a clear error or warning.
7. **JSON output**: --json on `timer show` returns an array, not an object. Document the breaking output shape in the changelog.
8. **Exomonad MCP probe**: grep exomonad for chainlink_timer_* tools and confirm they pass through an issue ID on both start and stop. If exomonad's MCP wrappers assume the singleton model anywhere, file a follow-up issue for exomonad.

## Verify
- cargo test in the chainlink crate — existing tests must pass (update assertions where the singleton was assumed)
- New unit tests:
  - Start timer for issue A, start timer for issue B, both active. `timer show` lists both.
  - Stop timer for issue A while issue B is still running. `timer show` lists only B.
  - `timer start A` while A is already running → error.
  - `timer stop A` when A has no active timer → error.
  - --all flag stops every active timer.
- Migration test: open a DB created by the pre-change binary, run the new binary, confirm existing timer history is intact and the new concurrent-start works.
- Manual: in a real session, `chainlink timer start 100`, `chainlink timer start 101`, `chainlink timer show`. Both visible. Stop one. Other still running.

## Done criteria
- Multiple concurrent timers coexist with no implicit auto-stop
- `timer start` / `timer stop` require an explicit issue ID
- `timer show` and `timer list` display all active timers
- A schema/migration is in place if needed; existing DBs upgrade cleanly
- Exomonad's TL can run `chainlink_timer_start` on every spawn and `chainlink_timer_stop` per child-completion without the timers interfering
- README/CLI help text updated to reflect the new per-issue model

## Why
The TL coordination model in exomonad assumes per-issue time tracking is concurrent — that's how scaffold-fork-converge produces parallelism gains. A singleton timer forces serialization of accounting that the actual work is doing in parallel, which means timer data is wrong and the TL can't use it for stuck-detection or budget tracking. This is the smallest upstream change that unblocks the orchestration.

issues.title: Worker pane cleanup: ensure the worker-pane-close feedback loop actually fires when a worker is done
issues.description:
## Problem

Workers are leaving their tmux panes open after the work is complete. Observed: TL receives the worker's notify_parent, processes the feedback (closes the chainlink issue, sometimes acts on it), but the worker's pane stays alive in the session.

Recent commit ea4600eb ("Add worker pane close feedback loop") was meant to address this. Either it does not fire in the path that occurred, or it fires but the actual kill-pane call does not reach tmux. Need investigation before adding a new cleanup path.

## Anti-patterns (FIRST)
- DO NOT couple chainlink_issue_close to tmux pane kill. The relationship is wrong-shape: a worker may address multiple issues, and an issue may be closed for reasons unrelated to a worker (e.g. TL closes after merging a leaf's PR). Lifecycle is per-worker, not per-issue.
- DO NOT add a second cleanup path that races with the existing one. Find why the existing loop did not fire and fix root cause.
- DO NOT silently kill a pane that has unsent output. Workers may emit useful diagnostic output between their final notify_parent and the pane close. Confirm output flushed (or persisted to a log) before kill.
- DO NOT mark a worker as "done" purely on TL acknowledgement. The worker process itself must reach a quiescent state — otherwise a still-running agent has its terminal yanked out from under it.
- DO NOT block the TL on worker cleanup. Cleanup is async; the TL keeps moving.

## Read first
- git show ea4600eb — the commit that introduced the close feedback loop. Touched files:
  - .exo/roles/devswarm/RootRole.hs, TLRole.hs
  - haskell/proto/src/Effects/Agent.hs (large change — new effect types)
  - haskell/wasm-guest/src/ExoMonad/Effects/Agent.hs
  - haskell/wasm-guest/src/ExoMonad/Guest/Effects/AgentControl.hs
  - haskell/wasm-guest/src/ExoMonad/Guest/Records/Spawn.hs
  - haskell/wasm-guest/src/ExoMonad/Guest/Tools/Spawn.hs
  - proto/effects/agent.proto
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/internal.rs:602-617 — worker pane creation site; pane_id is captured here but no obvious symmetrical close path
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/cleanup.rs — owns the cleanup pathway (named accordingly; verify what it actually does)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/tmux_events.rs and tmux_ipc.rs — tmux integration; look for kill-pane invocation
- .exo/roles/devswarm/context/root.md § Worker Correction Loop — TL's responsibilities when a worker reports blocked vs succeeded
- 0904b8ca ("Docs: sub-TL agent types and worker correction loop protocol") — recent doc update that may have changed expectations

## Investigation steps (do these before writing any fix)
1. Reproduce: spawn a worker with a trivial task ("echo done; exit"), capture the worker's notify_parent payload, observe whether the pane closes.
2. Tail the exomonad server log during reproduction. The close path almost certainly emits a tracing event — note whether kill-pane is logged at all, vs logged-and-failed, vs not invoked.
3. Determine where the feedback loop is supposed to trigger:
   - Is it on worker process exit (parent reaps the process)?
   - Is it on TL acknowledgement (TL responds to notify_parent)?
   - Is it on a worker-emitted "closing" effect?
4. Whichever it is, find the corresponding code site and add tracing breadcrumbs to confirm the path was entered.
5. Confirm pane_id is being persisted somewhere the close path can read. The internal.rs:602 pane_id capture has to flow into the cleanup pathway — verify the plumbing.

## Fix steps (after investigation pins the gap)
6. Implement the fix at the actual gap. Likely candidates:
   a. The worker process exits but the pane is not killed because tmux's "remain-on-exit" is on (or the agent process forks something that holds stdin open).
   b. The close feedback loop fires for sub-TL panes but not worker panes due to a role check.
   c. The pane_id is captured but not registered in the cleanup registry.
7. Whatever the fix, add the tracing line that proves it works to the log, and assert on it in a test (see Verify).
8. Decide explicitly what "closed" looks like for the user: does the pane vanish, or does it become a scrollback-only "completed" pane (tmux remain-on-exit pattern)? The former is cleaner; the latter is safer when debugging. Pick one and document.

## Verify
- cargo test -p exomonad-core (any new unit tests on the cleanup path)
- New integration test: spawn a worker that exits cleanly (test harness invokes a minimal codex/gemini-mock that writes notify_parent and exits), assert the pane is gone within N seconds (tmux list-panes does not contain it)
- New integration test: spawn a worker that errors out and exits non-zero, assert the same (failure path also cleans up — or assert opposite if we decide to keep failed panes for inspection; document the choice either way)
- Manual: real session, spawn a worker that runs a one-shot task. Worker completes. tmux list-panes confirms the pane is gone.

## Done criteria
- The reproduction case (worker reports done → pane stays) does not happen on the fixed code.
- A tracing breadcrumb at the kill-pane site proves the path was hit in the success case; on failure, a tracing::warn explains why kill-pane was skipped.
- The relationship between worker completion and pane cleanup is documented in CLAUDE.md or worker.md so future readers know the lifecycle invariant.
- chainlink_issue_close is NOT coupled to tmux. Pane lifecycle is owned exclusively by the worker lifecycle.

## Out of scope
- TL-implements-instead-of-redispatch is a separate issue (#TBD — TL role PreToolUse deny on edit tools).
- Sub-TL window cleanup is a separate concern (windows, not panes, different lifecycle).

## Why
A leaked pane per worker is a session-clutter UX paper cut today, but it scales badly. A long-running root TL that spawns dozens of workers fills the tmux session with stale panes. More importantly, the existence of stale panes hides bugs in agent process exit ("oh the worker is still there" can mask "oh the worker hung and is now zombie-attached to its pane"). Fixing this surfaces real failures faster.

Added wasm integration coverage that WorkerExit notifies parent and calls agent.close_self once. Verified: just check-fmt, just test-wasm-integration, just build.

issues.title: TL role: hard PreToolUse deny on Edit/Write/MultiEdit/NotebookEdit — TL must never implement
issues.description:
## Problem

TL agents (Opus) have been observed implementing code directly instead of dispatching to leaves/workers, after reading worker feedback. This breaks the exomonad cost model — Opus tokens are 10-30x leaf tokens, so any TL-authored line is wasted budget AND a violation of the architectural contract (TL plans, forks, merges; leaves implement).

Today the prohibition lives only in soft instructions:
- .exo/roles/devswarm/context/root.md: "You do not implement. You plan, fork, and merge."
- .claude/rules/exomonad.md: "TL never implements directly."
- CLAUDE.md § Cost Model: "Every token you spend on work a child could do is wasted."

Opus rationalizes around soft prompts ("just this one small fix", "the worker is stuck so I'll unblock it myself"). The guard needs to be uncircumventable at the hook layer.

## Anti-patterns (FIRST)
- DO NOT rely on prompt-level instructions alone. They have already proven insufficient.
- DO NOT deny tools at the runtime (Rust) layer. All hook/tool logic lives in Haskell WASM per architectural principle — see CLAUDE.md § "All Tools and Hooks in Haskell WASM".
- DO NOT block reads. TL legitimately uses Read, Grep, Glob, Bash (for git/gh inspection) constantly. Only mutating editor tools are forbidden.
- DO NOT include Bash in the deny list. TL needs bash for git/gh/chainlink calls. If bash-shell-edit avoidance becomes a problem, that is a separate, smaller scope.
- DO NOT use a TL allow-list ("only these tools allowed"). The set of legitimate TL tools grows; maintain a small deny-list of clearly-implementer tools instead.
- DO NOT exempt the root TL from the guard. The root is also a TL.
- DO NOT make the error message generic. The denial is the redispatch nudge — it should tell the TL exactly which spawn tool to use and link to the worker-correction-loop protocol.

## Read first
- .exo/roles/devswarm/Main.hs:37, 154-155 — handle_pre_tool_use FFI entry point
- .exo/roles/devswarm/TLRole.hs — TL role config (where the PreToolUse handler is composed for the TL role)
- .exo/roles/devswarm/RootRole.hs — root role config (same shape, also a TL)
- haskell/wasm-guest/src/ExoMonad/Guest/Tools/Spawn.hs:266-413 — existing allowed_tools / disallowed_tools machinery for spawned agents (precedent for tool-name filtering)
- CLAUDE.md § Tech Lead Praxis § Fire-and-Forget Execution — what TLs are supposed to do
- CLAUDE.md § "All Tools and Hooks in Haskell WASM" — architectural rule
- .exo/roles/devswarm/context/root.md § Worker Correction Loop — what TL should do when a worker is blocked

## Steps
1. In TLRole.hs and RootRole.hs, extend the PreToolUse hook config to deny a fixed set of tool names: Edit, Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit. The deny must short-circuit the tool call (HookEnvelope { exit_code = 2, stderr message visible to the agent }).
2. The denial message must be precise and actionable. Example body:
   > TL agents cannot use {tool_name}. The TL plans and dispatches; implementation belongs to leaves and workers.
   > If a leaf needs to fix code based on review feedback, the leaf does it (reviewer comments are injected into its pane automatically).
   > If a worker is blocked, use send_message to inject a clarification into the worker's pane (see Worker Correction Loop in root.md).
   > If neither path fits, re-decompose with spawn_leaf or spawn_worker.
   > See CLAUDE.md § Tech Lead Praxis for the full protocol.
3. Add a feature test: a TLRole instance fed a PreToolUse hook input for tool_name="Edit" returns exit_code=2 with the canonical message. Repeat for Write, MultiEdit, NotebookEdit. Repeat for RootRole.
4. Add a negative test: same role, tool_name="Read" / "Grep" / "Bash" / "spawn_leaf" → not denied (exit_code=0, no message).
5. Update .exo/roles/devswarm/context/root.md and .claude/rules/exomonad.md to reference the hard guard — note that the deny IS the redispatch nudge and that the TL should follow the denial message's instructions.
6. Confirm DevRole.hs and WorkerRole.hs are unaffected — leaves and workers DO need Edit/Write.

## Verify
- cabal test all (Haskell unit tests pick up the new role-level hook configs)
- E2E: spawn a TL, inject a synthetic PreToolUse hook event for tool_name="Edit" via the UDS hook endpoint, assert exit_code=2 and the canonical message in stderr
- Manual: bring up a session, ask the TL to "go fix this typo in foo.rs yourself" — assert the TL receives the deny on its first Edit attempt and pivots to spawn_worker
- Manual: TL legitimately runs git status, gh pr view, chainlink issue show — none blocked

## Done criteria
- TL and root roles cannot invoke Edit / Write / MultiEdit / NotebookEdit. Hook returns exit_code=2 with the canonical redispatch message.
- DevRole and WorkerRole are unchanged — leaves and workers retain full edit privileges.
- Unit + e2e tests pin both the deny and the allow cases.
- root.md and exomonad.md reference the guard so future TLs (and reviewers reading the rules) know the deny is structural, not a suggestion.

## Why
The exomonad architecture only works if the cost gradient holds (Opus plans, Gemini implements). Every Opus-authored line is a budget violation; every TL that does the work itself is a leaf that didn't get spawned (so the work isn't reviewed, isn't PR'd, isn't merge-gated). issues.title: Canonical knot hostname: detect what knot stamps, normalize everywhere on exomonad side
issues.description:
## Problem

Spindle drops CI events with: `error processing message ... err="repo knot does not match event source: localhost:5555 != localhost"`. This blocks merge-ready signals — PRs sit approved with CI never confirmed.

Root cause is asymmetric hostname normalization in rust/exomonad/src/init.rs:1311-1317:
```rust
let knot_hostname = config.tangled_knot_url
    .as_deref().unwrap_or("localhost:5555")
    .trim_start_matches("ws://")
    .trim_start_matches("wss://")
    .to_string();
```
This strips ws/wss only — not http/https — so the canonical CLAUDE.md example value `tangled_knot_url = "http://localhost:5555"` leaves the literal string `http://localhost:5555` flowing into the spindle source config, the SQL knot column, and the cursor seed. Meanwhile the knot binary inside the docker container stamps AT-proto events with whatever its own runtime hostname is (often bare `localhost`). The two sides never line up.

## Constraint

Do NOT modify the tangled-knot docker container, its compose file, or its env. The container is third-party config and must work as shipped. The fix lives entirely on the exomonad side: discover what the knot already stamps, then use that canonical form in every exomonad-owned string that compares against a knot identity.

## Anti-patterns (FIRST)
- DO NOT add an env var to the knot container (KNOT_HOSTNAME or similar). Container config is untouched per requirement.
- DO NOT hand-roll yet another scheme-stripping closure inline. One canonical normalizer, called from every site.
- DO NOT guess the knot's stamped hostname from the URL. Read what the knot actually uses — its own DB or its own /xrpc endpoint — and trust that.
- DO NOT silently fall back to a default when discovery fails. Log a clear error and surface it; a wrong default produces the exact bug we're fixing.
- DO NOT change the public config field name. `tangled_knot_url` stays the user-facing field; canonicalization is internal.

## Read first
- rust/exomonad/src/init.rs:1289-1450 — register_tangled_repo flow
- rust/exomonad/src/init.rs:1311-1317 — broken normalization
- rust/exomonad/src/init.rs:1519-1570 — seed_spindle_knot_cursor (also takes knot_hostname)
- rust/exomonad/src/init.rs:1680-1699 — tangled_dev_repo_did (already strips http/https correctly — this is the only consistent normalizer in the file; it should be lifted out)
- CLAUDE.md § Configuration — `tangled_knot_url` is documented as http:// form
- The spindle log line in the issue trigger: `localhost:5555 != localhost` proves the asymmetry

## Steps
1. Add canonical_knot_hostname(knot_db_path_or_container: &str) -> Result<String, KnotDiscoveryError> in a new module rust/exomonad-core/src/tangled.rs (or inline in init.rs if it stays one site). It opens the knot's SQLite DB (the path is already known from container inspection or from a configured tangled_knot_db field — add the field if missing) and reads the canonical knot hostname from wherever knot itself records it (likely a `repos` or `knot` table, or a config row). Document the query.
2. If reading from the knot DB is impractical, fall back to a single HTTP GET to the knot's identity endpoint (e.g. http://{knot_url}/xrpc/sh.tangled.knot.getInfo or whatever the knot exposes). One discovery call at registration time, result cached for the session.
3. Add a normalize_knot_hostname(raw: &str) -> String helper that strips ws/wss/http/https scheme + trailing slash + lowercases — same shape as the existing logic inside tangled_dev_repo_did:1681-1687. Make it pub(crate) and call it from every site that handled a knot string before this PR.
4. Replace the inline strip at init.rs:1311-1317 with: first try canonical_knot_hostname (discovery); on failure, fall back to normalize_knot_hostname(config.tangled_knot_url) and log a warn that consistency depends on the URL matching what knot stamps.
5. Update tangled_dev_repo_did to call normalize_knot_hostname instead of inlining the trim chain (DRY).
6. Update seed_spindle_knot_cursor and any other site using knot_hostname to receive the canonical form (compiler will guide).
7. Add a unit test matrix for normalize_knot_hostname: ws://, wss://, http://, https://, with and without ports, with and without trailing slash, mixed case. Assert all reduce to lowercase host[:port].
8. Add an integration test (or e2e if cheaper) that registers a repo, queries the spindle DB, and asserts the stored knot column equals the value the knot actually stamps into events.

## Verify
- cargo test -p exomonad — unit tests for normalize_knot_hostname
- Manual: in a fresh workspace with tangled_knot_url = "http://localhost:5555", run exomonad init → register_tangled_repo → push a commit → confirm spindle log shows no "repo knot does not match event source" error
- Manual: same with tangled_knot_url = "ws://localhost:5555" → identical behavior
- Manual: same with tangled_knot_url = "localhost:5555" (no scheme) → identical behavior

## Done criteria
- The error "repo knot does not match event source" cannot occur for any valid form of tangled_knot_url (with/without scheme, with/without port, with/without trailing slash)
- normalize_knot_hostname is the only place in the codebase that strips schemes from knot strings
- A unit test enumerates the URL-form matrix and asserts identical canonical output
- An integration test proves spindle accepts events from a freshly-registered repo
- CLAUDE.md § Configuration adds a one-line note that knot identity discovery is automatic — users do not need to keep tangled_knot_url and the knot container's runtime hostname in lockstep

## Why
Today's CLAUDE.md example value (`tangled_knot_url = "http://localhost:5555"`) is the broken path. Anyone following the docs as written hits the merge-ready stall described in the bug report. The fix moves identity discovery out of "hope the strings happen to match" into "ask the knot what it actually calls itself."

Verified: just fmt, just test-fast, focused nix develop --command cargo test -p exomonad normalize_knot_hostname, just build. Note: just test-cargo-all is currently blocked by unrelated AgentInfo.pane_id fixture compile errors in proto/wasm integration tests.

Final verification after adding DID-normalization coverage: just fmt passed, focused nix develop --command cargo test -p exomonad knot_hostname passed (2 tests), just build passed. The running local knot container reports KNOT_SERVER_HOSTNAME=localhost, confirming the issue path this fix now discovers instead of deriving from http/ws URL text.

issues.title: exomonad new: scaffold .tangled/workflows/ci.yml with language-aware framing
issues.description:
## Anti-patterns (FIRST)
- DO NOT template substantive build steps (deps, manifest paths) — workspace-specific, wrong template silently passes CI without testing the right thing.
- DO NOT clobber an existing .tangled/workflows/ci.yml. Skip if present, log at info.
- DO NOT fail `exomonad new` if scaffolding the YAML fails — warn and continue. New must stay reliable.
- DO NOT infer language from files in vendor/, .exo/worktrees/, or subdirs. Only inspect the workspace root.
- DO NOT emit empty `steps:` or empty `dependencies:` blocks that parse as null. Use a commented TODO line instead so the file is valid YAML that obviously needs editing.

## Read first
- rust/exomonad/src/new.rs — current `exomonad new` flow and template-copy pattern
- rust/exomonad/src/init.rs — atomic file write pattern (tempfile + persist)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/codex_config.rs:191 — write_atomic helper if generalized
- CLAUDE.md § Configuration — how `exomonad new` copies .exo/rules/exomonad.md as a template precedent
- The tangled config example the user shared in conversation (rust + nixery + native graphics deps) — proves substantive steps are project-specific

## Steps
1. Add `scaffold_tangled_workflow(project_dir: &Path) -> std::io::Result<()>` in rust/exomonad/src/new.rs (or a new tangled_workflow.rs sibling module).
2. Detect language by checking workspace-root files only:
   - `Cargo.toml` present → rust
   - `cabal.project` or any `*.cabal` at root → haskell
   - `pyproject.toml` or `setup.py` → python
   - `package.json` → node
   - else → generic
3. Always emit the framing identically (this is the part backrooms was missing):
```yaml
engine: nixery
when:
  - event: [push, manual]
    branch: ["*"]
  - event: [pull_request]
    branch: [main]
clone:
  depth: 1
  submodules: false
```
4. Append a language-flavored `dependencies.nixpkgs:` list with the minimum to bootstrap that toolchain (rust: rustup pkg-config; haskell: ghc cabal-install pkg-config; python: python3; node: nodejs; generic: empty list with comment).
5. Append a `steps:` block with a single placeholder step whose `command:` is a commented `# TODO` line explaining what to fill in, plus a link to docs/decisions on tangled-CI (or the relevant CLAUDE.md section).
6. Use atomic write (tempfile + persist into the .tangled/workflows/ directory). Create parent dirs.
7. Skip if .tangled/workflows/ci.yml exists. Log: "tangled workflow already present at <path>, leaving untouched".
8. Wire the call into the existing `exomonad new` flow alongside the existing template copies. On error, log warn and continue — do not abort `new`.

## Verify
- `cargo test -p exomonad` — existing tests must still pass
- New unit test: feed each detected-language branch through scaffold_tangled_workflow into a tempdir, assert (a) file exists, (b) parses as valid YAML via serde_yaml or equivalent, (c) contains the framing literally, (d) idempotent on second call (no clobber)
- Manual: `exomonad new` in a fresh tempdir with a Cargo.toml present → asserts rust-flavored file is created; rerun → no change

## Done criteria
- Fresh workspace with Cargo.toml at root → `exomonad new` creates .tangled/workflows/ci.yml with rust framing + TODO steps
- Fresh workspace with no language marker → file with generic framing + TODO steps
- Re-running `exomonad new` on a workspace that already has .tangled/workflows/ci.yml leaves it untouched
- Scaffold failure does not abort `exomonad new` (logged warning, continue)
- Unit test suite covers all five language branches plus the idempotency case
- CLAUDE.md "Configuration" section updated to mention the tangled scaffold next to the rules template

## Why
Backrooms project landed bugs because the tangled framing (`engine: nixery`, `when:`, `clone:`) was missing, not because the build steps were wrong. Framing is universal and safe to template; build steps stay workspace-specific by design.

issues.description:

- In the CI-success recovery path added by #186: emit [MERGE READY: #N ci=success] not just [CI NOW PASSING]
- WASM event handler for 'ci_status' kind='success' should check reviewer_approved state and route accordingly

       haskell/wasm-guest/src/ExoMonad/Guest/Events.hs (event handler return)

Update E2E status next test marker

Bug: ci_status transition to Success silently dropped after notified_parent_approved
issues.description:
In worktree_event_watcher.rs compute_pr_actions(), there is an early-return guard:

  if old_state.notified_parent_approved || old_state.notified_parent_timeout {
      return pending_actions;  // empty
  }

This guard fires correctly once the TL is notified. But when:
1. Reviewer approves while CI is still Pending → notified_parent_approved = true → [PR READY] sent to TL
2. TL calls merge_pr → CI gate blocks the merge (status != Success)
3. CI later transitions to Success
4. Watcher fires ci_status WasmEvent → guard returns empty immediately → TL never hears about it

The TL is stuck waiting for a [MERGE READY] that will never arrive. Merge gate enforces CI but there is no recovery notification path once notified_parent_approved has suppressed all further events.

Fix: track a new state field merge_blocked_on_ci. When merge_pr returns a CI-gate error, set it. When ci_status transitions to Success and merge_blocked_on_ci is true, emit notify_parent regardless of the notified_parent_approved guard.

Files: rust/exomonad-core/src/services/worktree_event_watcher.rs (compute_pr_actions, WatchState)
       rust/exomonad-core/src/services/merge_pr_local.rs (CI gate response path)

issues.description:
Design the full integration based on investigation findings (blocks on investigation issue).

Proposed design:

ExoMonad birth-branch/worktree identity is the coordination mechanism; Chainlink locks conflict with that model and do not add needed functionality. Revised design should focus only on timer lifecycle and separately investigate whether chainlink agent identity adds useful audit correlation.

Design revision: remove both Chainlink locks and Chainlink agent commands from the proposed integration. ExoMonad should not call chainlink agent init/status or chainlink locks claim/release for spawned tasks. Remaining viable design area is TL-only chainlink timer support that directly calls timer commands and avoids session_work/lock paths.

issues.title: Investigation: chainlink agent/lock/timer attribution scope
issues.description:
Answer three questions before designing the spawn integration:

1. Does 'chainlink agent init <ID>' write to the worktree-local .chainlink/ config or to the shared sqlite DB? If shared, multiple worktrees collide on identity; if local, each worktree gets its own identity cleanly.

2. Does 'chainlink locks claim <issue>' record which agent_id holds the lock? Current lock JSON shows {"locks":{}} — need to verify if agent attribution is stored.

3. Can spawn.rs reliably call 'chainlink agent init <birth-branch>' from the new worktree directory before the agent process starts — same pattern as writing .mcp.json and settings.local.json?

4. Does 'chainlink timer start <issue>' integrate with the sessions table or is it a separate time_entries row only?

Output: short ADR in docs/decisions/ with findings and go/no-go recommendation for auto-init.

comments.content: Finding: the Chainlink lock backend creates a git worktree at .chainlink/.locks-cache on fixed branch chainlink/locks. This conflicts with ExoMonad's current assumption that registered worktree branches are agent birth branches / identity-bearing branches. Running chainlink locks list --json is enough to recreate the worktree/branch in the project repo, so lock state should be moved out of the main repo's git worktree namespace or explicitly filtered from agent/worktree discovery.

Decision: do not integrate Chainlink locks into ExoMonad spawned-task workflow. ExoMonad's git birth-branch naming already provides the coordination semantics we need: preventing dev/worker stomping across TL-managed work and allowing spawned workers to share/operate within the intended git worktree model. Chainlink's lock backend currently creates its own git worktree/branch (chainlink/locks), which conflicts with branch-as-agent-identity semantics. Adding lock claim/release around spawned tasks would not add useful functionality here unless Chainlink changes its lock semantics/storage model. Treat lock support as out of scope for this integration.

Additional no-go criterion: if chainlink timer functionality is coupled to Chainlink locks internally, timer integration should be rejected too. The acceptable path is timer-only audit data with no lock backend involvement, no lock worktree creation, and no chainlink/locks branch.

Final integration decision: drop both Chainlink lock and Chainlink agent command integration from ExoMonad MCP. Both conflict with ExoMonad's git birth-branch identity/coordination model. Timer remains useful only as TL-owned lifecycle tracking and only if independent of locks.

Investigation output: docs/decisions/chainlink-agent-timer-lock-scope.md. Result: drop Chainlink locks and Chainlink agent command MCP integration; create new scoped timer task #196 for TL-only timer lifecycle tracking.

issues.title: Research: codex exec review subcommand behavior and integration requirements
issues.description:
Question: 

Context: 

Findings: 

## Goal

Understand the codex exec review subcommand well enough to implement Codex reviewer integration correctly in spawn_reviewer_subtree.

## What we know

docs/decisions/codex-integration.md documents the command:

    codex exec review --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --cd <worktree_dir>

This is listed as the correct command for Codex reviewer agents instead of wrapping reviewer instructions in a generic codex exec prompt. Issue #160 covers the implementation, but needs this research first.

## Questions to answer

1. What does codex exec review do differently from codex exec with a reviewer prompt?
   - Does it have built-in review heuristics, or is it prompt-driven?
   - What output does it produce — structured JSON, markdown, or free-form?

2. How does it write review output? Does it:
   - Write to .exo/reviews/pr_N.json (exomonad convention) automatically?
   - Write to a codex-native location?
   - Or does the reviewer agent write it via tool calls?

3. Does it accept a base branch / PR branch as arguments, or does it infer from git state?

4. Does it have a --model flag like codex exec does?

5. What is the exit code behavior — does it signal approve vs changes-requested?

6. Does codex exec review need reviewer-specific developer_instructions in .codex/config.toml, or does the subcommand handle framing internally?

7. Is there a way to pass the PR number or review context (title, author) so the reviewer knows what it is reviewing?

## Investigation method

- Run codex exec review --help in the codex source or against the binary
- Check codex-rs source in /home/goya/agent-workspace/codex if available
- Run a smoke test against a test PR in a sandbox repo

## Feeds into

Issue #160 (spawn_reviewer_subtree Codex implementation)
Issue #159 (CODEX_REVIEWER_INSTRUCTIONS)

comments.content:
Findings from local Codex CLI/source research:

1. `codex exec review` exists and supports: positional custom prompt, `--uncommitted`, `--base <BRANCH>`, `--commit <SHA>`, `--title <TITLE>` (commit-only), `--model <MODEL>`, `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`, `--json`, and `--output-last-message <FILE>`.

2. Target selection is mutually exclusive: `--base`, `--commit`, `--uncommitted`, and positional prompt conflict with each other. If none is supplied, CLI errors: "Specify --uncommitted, --base, --commit, or provide custom review instructions".

3. `--base <BRANCH>` builds a review target that resolves merge-base with HEAD and prompts Codex to run `git diff <merge_base_sha>`. That is the right primitive for ExoMonad reviewer worktrees when HEAD is the worker PR branch/detached checkout and the base branch is known.

4. Output is Codex review-mode output, not ExoMonad review state. Internally the reviewer is asked to produce `ReviewOutputEvent` JSON; the exec/app-server layer renders it as plain text in an `ExitedReviewMode` event and as the final assistant message. `--json` streams JSONL events, but the review payload is still Codex-native; it does not write `.exo/reviews/pr_N.json`.

5. Exit code is automation success/failure only. It exits nonzero on server/turn failure or interrupt, not approve vs changes-requested.

6. `codex exec review` uses Codex's built-in review rubric from `core/review_prompt.md` and review task code sets review base instructions internally. It does not by itself know ExoMonad PR number, author, or the `.exo/reviews/pr_N.json` convention. ExoMonad still needs either: (a) run reviewer as normal Codex agent with CODEX_REVIEWER_INSTRUCTIONS and MCP review tools, or (b) run `codex exec review --base <base> --output-last-message <file>` and post-process the output into `.exo/reviews/pr_N.json`.

Recommendation for #160: do not replace the reviewer path with bare `codex exec review --base <base>` unless #160 also adds a translator from Codex review output to ExoMonad review files. The simpler safe implementation is to keep Codex reviewer instructions/tool calls as the authority, or use `codex exec review` only with an output file plus explicit post-processing.

issues.title: Block direct sqlite3 access to .chainlink/ in dev role permissionCascade
issues.description:
Goal: 

Acceptance criteria:
- 

## Problem

When dev agents lack chainlink MCP tools, they fall back to direct sqlite3 access against .chainlink/issues.db. The permissionCascade in .exo/lib/HttpDevHooks.hs already intercepts all PreToolUse events for dev agents but checkAgentPermissions is a stub that returns Allowed unconditionally (ExoMonad.Permissions:92).

We need a guard that detects shell commands targeting .chainlink/ directly and blocks them with a helpful redirect to the MCP tools.

## Fix

In permissionCascade in .exo/lib/HttpDevHooks.hs, add a shell command guard before the checkAgentPermissions call:

1. Extract the command string from tool_input when tool_name is a shell tool ("shell", "run_command", "computer", or tool_input has a "command" key)
2. Check if the command contains "sqlite3" and ".chainlink":
   
   checkChainlinkSqlAccess :: HookInput -> Maybe Text
   checkChainlinkSqlAccess hookInput =
     case hiToolInput hookInput of
       Just (Object obj)
         | Just (String cmd) <- KM.lookup "command" obj
         , "sqlite3" `T.isInfixOf` cmd
         , ".chainlink" `T.isInfixOf` cmd
         -> Just "BLOCKED: Do not access .chainlink/issues.db directly via sqlite3. Use the chainlink MCP tools (chainlink_issue_show, chainlink_issue_close) instead."
       _ -> Nothing

3. Add to permissionCascade before checkAgentPermissions:
   case checkChainlinkSqlAccess hookInput of
     Just reason -> pure (denyResponse reason)
     Nothing -> ... (existing checkAgentPermissions path)

This applies to dev role only (httpDevHooks). Worker role has chainlink MCP tools available so workers are less likely to need this guard, but a similar rule could be added to WorkerRole preToolUse if needed.

## Files

- .exo/lib/HttpDevHooks.hs (add checkChainlinkSqlAccess, wire into permissionCascade)

## Depends on

Issue #161 is the structural fix; this is the defensive guard. Both are needed.

issues.title: Use codex exec review in spawn_reviewer_subtree for Codex reviewer agents
issues.description:
Goal: 

Acceptance criteria:
- 

## Problem

spawn_reviewer_subtree (rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/spawn.rs:1214-1289) calls generic spawn_subtree for all reviewer agent types including Codex. For Codex, this generates:

    codex exec --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --cd <dir> "$(cat <prompt_file>)"

But codex-integration.md explicitly documents a native review subcommand:

    codex exec review --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --cd <worktree_dir>

The native subcommand is designed for code review and should be used instead of wrapping review instructions into a generic exec prompt.

## Fix

Add a Codex-specific branch in spawn_reviewer_subtree before the call to spawn_subtree. When reviewer_agent_type is Codex:

1. Skip spawn_subtree — build the codex exec review command directly via build_codex_review_command (new helper)
2. Add build_codex_review_command in internal.rs:
   
    fn build_codex_review_command(worktree_dir: &Path, model: Option<&str>) -> String {
        let escaped_dir = Self::escape_for_shell_command(&worktree_dir.display().to_string());
        let model_flag = model.map(|m| format!(" --model {}", ...)).unwrap_or_default();
        format!("codex exec review --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --cd {}{}", escaped_dir, model_flag)
    }

3. Still write .codex/config.toml + hooks.json via write_codex_config_files (with reviewer instructions from issue #159)
4. Still create the worktree and register the agent via finalize_spawn

- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/internal.rs (add build_codex_review_command)
- rust/exomonad-core/src/services/agent_control/spawn.rs:1214-1289 (spawn_reviewer_subtree)

issues.title: Codex TL: hook review prompt appears when Codex is restarted manually after init
issues.description:
Steps to reproduce:
1. 

Expected: 
Actual: 

## Problem

When `exomonad init --tl codex` runs, the TL window command is:

    codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --cd <dir>

This correctly bypasses the hook review gate. However, there is no `; exec bash -l` fallback (unlike Claude which has `|| claude ...; echo; echo [Claude Code exited]; exec bash -l`).

When Codex exits, the user drops to the shell and restarts with bare `codex`. The .codex/config.toml sets `approval_policy = "never"` (YOLO mode), which bypasses tool approvals but NOT hook review. Hook review requires `--dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox`. Result: PreToolUse, PostToolUse, and Stop hooks land in the review queue.

## Fix

Change `build_codex_root_command` in `rust/exomonad/src/init.rs` (lines 75-94) to add a shell fallback:

    format!(
        "codex --dangerously-bypass-approvals-and-sandbox --cd {}{}{}; exec bash -l",
        escaped_dir, model_flag, prompt
    )

Mirrors the Claude TL pattern. When Codex exits the user lands in a shell with the correct CWD.

## File

rust/exomonad/src/init.rs — build_codex_root_command (lines 75-94)

Goal:

    [hook] decision=allow exit_code=0 tool=file_pr

issues.title: Implement explicit allow/deny handling in OpenCode plugin tool.execute.before
issues.description:
Goal: 

Acceptance criteria:
- 

The current OpenCode plugin (rust/exomonad-core/src/opencode_plugin.rs) reads WASM response args but does not act on the allow/deny signal at all. Both allow and deny paths are implicit (no-op = allow, blocked = never).

Implement full allow/deny logic in tool.execute.before:

ALLOW path ({"continue": true}):
- Merge modified args from WASM response into output.args if present
- Otherwise pass through unchanged
- Confirm the tool proceeds normally

DENY path ({"continue": false}):
- Block the tool call via OpenCode plugin API (check 1.14.48 docs — may require throwing, returning a specific value, or setting output to null/undefined)
- Surface the reason from WASM response if present (check ClaudePreToolUseOutput for reason field)

This pairs with #137. Together they make the plugin a complete hook bridge rather than a partial one that only handles arg mutation.

Update OPENCODE_PLUGIN_TS const and docs/decisions/opencode-hooks.md.

- INFO: allow/deny decision and exit_code for ToolUse/Stop dispatches
- DEBUG: full request payload and WASM response
- Add EXOMONAD_HOOK_TRACE=1 env var to enable full request/response logging without recompile

Goal: 'exomonad serve 2>&1 | grep hook' shows a clear trace of every activation. Makes OpenCode hook bridge development observable.

When WASM returns a deny response (continue_: false, serialized as {"continue": false}), the plugin ignores it and lets the tool call proceed.

Add deny logic to tool.execute.before:
- Parse WASM response for {"continue": false}
- Surface the denial via OpenCode's plugin API (check 1.14.48 docs for how tool.execute.before can block a call)
- Update OPENCODE_PLUGIN_TS const in rust/exomonad-core/src/opencode_plugin.rs
- Update docs/decisions/opencode-hooks.md to document the deny mechanism

issues.title: OpenCode TL: auto-register supervisor at init so notify_parent delivery works without TeamCreate
issues.description:
Goal: 

Acceptance criteria:
- 

Claude TL calls TeamCreate (Claude Code native tool) to register a team, which wires up the Teams inbox delivery for notify_parent. OpenCode TL has no equivalent.

Current fallback: notify_parent without a team falls back to structural identity (birth-branch parent) → tmux injection to the TL window. This works but only if:
- The child agent's birth branch is correctly set so parent resolution works
- The TL window name ('TL') is stable and injectable

The 'No team found for agent — skipping supervisor registration' warning indicates the SupervisorRegistry is not populated, which breaks the notify_parent routing chain before it even reaches tmux fallback.

Fix options:
A. exomonad init (when root_agent_type == OpenCode): auto-call the session.register_team effect directly (without needing the agent to call TeamCreate). Register 'root' as the team lead for a synthetic team. This populates TeamRegistry so worker notify_parent can find the parent via team lookup.
B. Auto-register supervisor in spawn_subtree when spawning an OpenCode child: write the parent-child relationship to SupervisorRegistry directly so notify_parent resolution works without a team.
C. Ensure tmux injection path is robust enough as the sole fallback (no team needed).

Option B is cleanest: in spawn_subtree after creating the worktree, call self.ctx.supervisor_registry().register(child_name, parent_birth_branch). This mirrors what register_child_supervisor does but without requiring a team.

Branch: feat/spawn-tool-agnosticism

comments.content: Implemented the useful non-ACP part: spawned non-Claude children are registered in SupervisorRegistry by concrete agent ID, with a synthetic team fallback when no Claude TeamCreate context exists. notify_parent now checks supervisor by agent_id before the legacy birth-branch key, then falls back to structural identity/tmux routing.

issues.title: Investigate spindle event idempotency for persistent spindle.db across exomonad init sessions
issues.description:
Question: 

Context: 

Findings: 

## Question

Does spindle re-trigger nixery pipeline containers when it replays events on restart (cursor always backfills from 0)?

If idempotent → keep spindle.db persistent across exomonad init runs (repos table stays seeded, no re-seeding overhead, nixery layer cache already persists via Docker independently).
If not idempotent → delete spindle.db on each init to avoid duplicate pipeline runs.

## What to investigate

In tangled-core/cmd/spindle/ and tangled-core/pkg/spindle/ (or equivalent):

1. When spindle starts and backfills from cursor=0, does it re-process sh.tangled.pipeline events it has already executed?
2. Is there a completed-run table or deduplication key (e.g. rkey) that prevents re-triggering?
3. What is the cost of re-seeding the repos table vs keeping spindle.db persistent?
4. Are there any state consistency concerns with a long-lived spindle.db (e.g. stale repo entries, orphaned pipeline records)?

## Expected outcome

Establish a best practice:
- Option A: Persistent spindle.db (exomonad init never deletes it, only the e2e test does for isolation)
- Option B: Fresh spindle.db per init (exomonad init deletes and re-seeds on startup)
- Option C: Selective reset (preserve repos table, reset cursor tables only)

Note: nixery Docker layer cache is independent of spindle.db — downloads are already cached by Docker regardless of which option is chosen.

issues.title: Configurable PR reviewer agent in exomonad init (agent type, model, headless) + Tangled as local forge backend
issues.description:
Goal: 

Acceptance criteria:
- 

## Problem

The PR review convergence loop is hardcoded. There is no way to configure:
- Which agent type runs the reviewer (claude, opencode)
- Which model the reviewer uses
- What context files are injected into the reviewer session

The reviewer also always spawns a tmux window, which is unnecessary overhead given reviewer_max_rounds=2. It is short-lived and purely computational.

Additionally, the e2e test for PR review currently has no local forge backend — it would need a mock GitHub or a live GitHub token. The Tangled knot docker container (already used in e2e-tangled-ci) is a real git forge and should serve as the local forge backend for PR review e2e tests.

## Design

### 1. Reviewer config in config.toml

```toml
[reviewer]
agent_type = "claude"   # claude | opencode
model = "haiku"         # model flag passed to the reviewer agent
context = []             # list of context file paths to inject into reviewer session
```

exomonad init reads this block and passes reviewer identity/model to the WorktreeEventWatcher's ReviewerSpawner. Defaults: claude haiku, no extra context.

### 2. Headless reviewer (no tmux window)

ReviewerSpawner should spawn the reviewer as a background process (no tmux window), not as an interactive session. The reviewer reads the PR diff, posts a review via gh/Tangled API, and exits. Since max_rounds=2, there is no need for a persistent pane. The convergence loop drives it via the event watcher, not via a live terminal session.

### 3. Tangled as forge backend for e2e

For the e2e-pr-review test, replace mock GitHub with the Tangled knot docker container (same container used in e2e-tangled-ci). This requires:
- file_pr to support Tangled's PR/patch API (not just gh pr create)
- WorktreeEventWatcher to poll Tangled for PR state (review comments, approval, merge status)
- The forge backend should be pluggable: GitHub (default) or Tangled (when tangled_owner_did is set)

This gives a fully local dev environment: knot + spindle docker → CI, knot PR API → code review, no GitHub token needed.

### 4. e2e-pr-review test

New test: tests/e2e/pr-review/
- Uses Tangled knot as forge backend
- Worker pushes code, files PR via Tangled API
- WorktreeEventWatcher detects new PR, spawns headless reviewer
- Reviewer posts review (approve or request changes)
- Convergence loop resolves
- TL receives [PR READY] or [STUCK] notification
- Test asserts correct notification was delivered

## Dependencies
- Tangled PR API integration (file_pr + watcher polling)
- Headless reviewer spawner (no tmux window)
- Reviewer config block in config.toml + exomonad init wiring

Goal: 

Acceptance criteria:
-

Template at ~/.exo/tangled.toml (copied from a default during 'just install-all'):
  knot_url    = "ws://localhost:5555"
  spindle_url = "ws://localhost:6555"
  owner_did   = "did:plc:localdev"

exomonad new behaviour (addition):
1. Check if ~/.exo/tangled.toml exists
2. If yes, read knot_url / spindle_url / owner_did and write them into the generated .exo/config.toml:
     tangled_knot_url    = "<knot_url>"
     tangled_spindle_url = "<spindle_url>"
   (owner_did is not in config.toml today — add it as tangled_owner_did for use by exomonad init XRPC calls)
3. repo_name is auto-detected from the workspace directory name (no user input needed)
4. If ~/.exo/tangled.toml is absent, skip silently — tangled integration is opt-in

The template file itself ships as a default at ~/.exo/tangled.toml.default (written by 'just install-all') so users can: cp ~/.exo/tangled.toml.default ~/.exo/tangled.toml and fill in their DID.

issues.title: exomonad init: auto-register repo with tangled knot when tangled_knot_url is configured
issues.description:
When tangled_knot_url and tangled_owner_did are present in .exo/config.toml (written by exomonad new from ~/.exo/tangled.toml), exomonad init should automatically register the current repo with the knot via XRPC. This replaces the manual setup-dev.sh workflow and means a real 'git push tangled' from any agent worktree triggers the full knot guard -> pipeline event -> spindle CI chain.

Design:
1. During 'exomonad init', if tangled_knot_url and tangled_owner_did are in config:
   a. Call sh.tangled.knot.getRepo XRPC — if repo exists, skip
   b. Call sh.tangled.knot.createRepo XRPC — registers repo so post-receive hook fires on SSH pushes
   c. Set git remote 'tangled' to the knot SSH URL for this repo
2. New TangledService in rust/exomonad-core/src/services/ handles XRPC calls
3. repo_name auto-detected from workspace directory name (same source as exomonad new)
4. Log all steps (before/after/error per CLAUDE.md logging rules)

Idempotent: getRepo check means re-running exomonad init is safe.

Depends on: #111 (global tangled config + exomonad new writes tangled_owner_did into config.toml)

issues.title: Investigate existing RunProcess/ExecCommand effect in wasm-guest Effects/
issues.description: Read all files in haskell/wasm-guest/src/ExoMonad/Guest/Effects/. Determine if a general RunProcess or ExecCommand effect already exists. If yes: document the type signature and host function name. If no: plan ChainlinkExec as new effect. Output: a comment on this issue stating finding + decision. Blocks B2.

comments.content:
**Finding:** A general process execution effect already exists — `ExoMonad.Effects.Process` / `ProcessRun` with `effectId = "process.run"`. Full details:

- **Input:** `RunRequest { command, args, working_dir (relative only), env, timeout_ms }`
- **Output:** `RunResponse { exit_code, stdout, stderr }`
- **Usage:** Called via `suspendEffect @ProcessRun` from tool handlers (MergePR.hs, TestRunner.hs)
- **No Guest wrapper:** Unlike AgentControl/FileSystem, there is no `ExoMonad.Guest.Effects.Process` module — tool handlers call `suspendEffect @ProcessRun` directly.

**Decision:** Option A (use `ProcessRun` directly) is sufficient for ChainlinkExec. Chainlink commands like `chainlink create`, `chainlink subissue`, `chainlink close` etc. can be invoked the same way `git pull` and `./post_review.sh` currently are. No new `ExoMonad.Guest.Effects.Chainlink` module needed unless structured chainlink output parsing is required at the effect level (rather than in tool handler code).

**Zero existing chainlink code in haskell/ directory.**

issues.title: Thread --model into worker-pane build_agent_command for OpenCode
Add exomonad models discovery subcommand
issues.description:
## Goal

exomonad models [harness] [provider]

Lists available models per agent harness so users can pick values for
--tl-model and --worker-model without leaving the terminal.

## Harness Support (discovered empirically)

| Harness  | Discovery | Command             | Output format        |
|----------|-----------|---------------------|----------------------|
| opencode | Native    | opencode models [p] | provider/model lines |
| gemini   | None      | N/A                 | static list          |
| claude   | None      | N/A                 | static list          |

## Command Shape

  exomonad models                      # all harnesses
  exomonad models opencode             # opencode only (all providers)
  exomonad models opencode <provider>  # filtered by provider

## Files

  rust/exomonad/src/main.rs    add Models subcommand to Commands enum
  rust/exomonad/src/models.rs  new file, all implementation

## Implementation

### 1. CLI (main.rs)

Add to Commands enum:

  /// List available models per agent harness.
  Models {
      /// Harness to query: opencode, gemini, or claude. Omit for all.
      #[arg(value_name = "HARNESS")]
      harness: Option<String>,
      /// Provider filter (opencode only). E.g. "anthropic", "openai".
      #[arg(value_name = "PROVIDER")]
      provider: Option<String>,
  },

Wire to: models::run(harness, provider).await

### 2. Implementation (models.rs)

pub async fn run(harness: Option<String>, provider: Option<String>) -> Result<()>

Match on harness:
  None              => run_all(provider).await
  Some("opencode")  => run_opencode(provider).await
  Some("gemini")    => run_gemini().await
  Some("claude")    => run_claude().await
  Some(other)       => bail!("Unknown harness: {other}. Valid: opencode, gemini, claude")

run_opencode(provider: Option<String>):
  Build argv: ["opencode", "models"] + provider.as_slice()
  Exec with .stdout(Stdio::inherit()) -- stream directly, no buffering
  On non-zero exit, bail! with stderr

run_gemini():
  Print static list of known model IDs:
    gemini-2.5-pro, gemini-2.0-flash, gemini-2.0-flash-lite
  Print note: "Gemini does not expose model discovery. List may be stale."

run_claude():
  Print static list:
    claude-opus-4-7, claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-haiku-4-5-20251001
  Print note: "Use shorthand (opus, sonnet, haiku) or full ID with --tl-model."

run_all(provider):
  Print "# opencode", then run_opencode(provider)
  Print "# gemini",   then run_gemini()
  Print "# claude",   then run_claude()

## Verify

  exomonad models
    prints sections: opencode (live stream), gemini (static), claude (static)
  exomonad models opencode
    streams opencode models output directly
  exomonad models opencode anthropic
    filters to anthropic/* models via opencode CLI
  exomonad models gemini
    static list + staleness note
  exomonad models badharness
    error: Unknown harness: badharness. Valid: opencode, gemini, claude

## Out of scope

  Caching model lists
  Gemini API-based discovery (requires GEMINI_API_KEY, no stable CLI)
  Per-model validation at init time (separate issue)

Steps to reproduce:

## Problem

The TL prompt (You are the root TL.md) tells the agent to verify fork_wave success by checking tmux list-windows for a -opencode suffix. But OpenCode workers are headless ACP processes (background opencode serve --port 0) and never create tmux windows. The check always fails even on a correct spawn.

Sanity check the new behavior on the FIRST spawn:

  tmux list-windows for them -- it will always be empty for opencode workers.

  To observe a worker's progress: ps aux | grep 'opencode serve'
  To manually nudge a stuck worker: opencode run --attach <url> your message

OpenCode ACP spawn flow:

2. Port is captured from stdout
3. Task delivered via opencode run --attach <url>

issues.title: Fix --worker flag ignored — spawn_worker falls back to hardcoded Gemini

issues.description:

issues.title: fork_wave/spawn_subtree handler ignores config.spawn_agent_type (hardcodes Claude fallback)
issues.description:
Steps to reproduce:
1. 

Expected: 
Actual: 

Same bug class as spawn_worker, different default value.

ROOT CAUSE: In rust/exomonad-core/src/handlers/agent.rs, the fork_wave/spawn_subtree handler path uses 'unwrap_or(ServiceAgentType::Claude)' (or similar) when the proto agent_type is unspecified. Haskell side defaults fwcAgentType to AC.Claude via fromMaybe (Spawn.hs:134), so the proto field is often unset.

FIX: Replace the hardcoded Claude fallback with self.agent_control.default_spawn_agent_type(), the same pattern as the spawn_worker fix. This makes --worker=opencode cover both spawn_worker AND fork_wave uniformly.

Search rust/exomonad-core/src/handlers/agent.rs for: convert_agent_type(.*).unwrap_or
Apply the config-default pattern at every match in the spawn handler family.

DEPENDS ON: 'Add default_spawn_agent_type() getter' issue.

issues.title: spawn_worker handler ignores config.spawn_agent_type (hardcodes Gemini fallback)
issues.description:
Steps to reproduce:
1. 

Expected: 
Actual: 

BUG: When user runs 'exomonad init --worker=opencode', spawned workers still come up as Gemini. Server logs show 'mvp-room-gemini' instead of 'mvp-room-opencode'.

ROOT CAUSE: rust/exomonad-core/src/handlers/agent.rs:376 has:
  agent_type: convert_agent_type(req.agent_type()).unwrap_or(ServiceAgentType::Gemini)

The hardcoded Gemini fallback ignores config.spawn_agent_type, even though the config IS passed into AgentControlService at serve.rs:941 via with_spawn_agent_type().

FIX: Replace the unwrap_or with the configured default:
  let default_type = self.agent_control.default_spawn_agent_type();
  agent_type: convert_agent_type(req.agent_type()).unwrap_or(default_type),

DEPENDS ON: 'Add default_spawn_agent_type() getter' issue.

VERIFICATION: After fix, 'exomonad init --worker=opencode' followed by spawn_worker call should produce a tmux pane named 'name-opencode' (not 'name-gemini').

issues.title: spawn_worker ignores agent_type: hardcodes AgentType::Gemini in Rust
issues.description:
Current state: 

Desired state: 

Reason: 

SpawnWorkerRequest proto has no agent_type field (SpawnSubtreeRequest does). Haskell tool sends agent_type in payload but Rust ignores it.
